My vision has become blurred, and I’m having trouble getting some words out, although I know what I want to say. I also feel unusually tired and unsteady. I have type 2 diabetes, but I have not had symptoms like this before. Over the past several months, I’ve noticed that fatigue becomes much worse when I get overheated, such as during long walks across campus. I have not fainted or had any injury today. Please let the team know these symptoms started suddenly.

Symptoms: right-sided arm and leg weakness; numbness in the right hand; blurred vision; trouble finding words; unsteady balance; nausea; headache
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 42-year-old man who works at a daycare and arrived alone after coworkers called for help. He reports about a day of worsening right arm and leg weakness, with numbness most noticeable in the right hand. He has had intermittent blurred vision and trouble finding words, and says he feels unsteady when walking. He also reports nausea and a headache but no reported loss of consciousness. History includes high blood pressure, cigarette use, and several episodes of visual disturbance years ago that were never given a clear explanation. Symptoms reportedly fluctuated while he was at work.

Symptoms: Left-sided arm and leg weakness; tingling of the left cheek and hand; intermittent blurred vision; brief slurred speech; headache
Case_History_Text: A 29-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after arriving alone from her workplace. She reports that she first noticed tingling in her left hand and cheek last night, followed by a sense of heaviness and reduced strength in the left arm and leg. She had a headache developing over the same period, described as pressure across the forehead without vomiting. This morning, her vision became intermittently blurred, more noticeable when reading, and she had several minutes of slurred speech during a phone conversation. The speech difficulty resolved before arrival, but the left-sided symptoms and visual disturbance have persisted. She denies falling, loss of consciousness, or recent head injury. Her history includes high blood pressure, though she is uncertain of her recent readings and acknowledges occasionally missing medication. She works as an office administrator and had been under increased deadline-related stress this week. She reports no similar prior episode.

Symptoms: intermittent right-arm numbness and weakness; blurred vision; trouble keeping balance; difficulty finding words
Case_History_Text: I’m 45 and use they/them pronouns. I work as a cook at a busy restaurant, and my coworker came with me after EMS was called. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had spells where my right arm feels numb and weak, my vision gets blurred, and I have trouble keeping my balance. A few times I knew what I wanted to say but had difficulty getting the words out. The episodes come and go, and I feel mostly better between them, though my arm still feels unusual now. I’ve had a couple of similar, shorter spells in the past that went away on their own, but I was never given a clear explanation. I’ve been sleeping very little during several recent shifts and otherwise have felt well.

Symptoms: left arm numbness and weakness; blurred vision; brief slurred speech; fatigue; nausea
Case_History_Text: 26-year-old woman, security guard, arrived alone after leaving work. Reports left arm tingling and reduced grip beginning earlier today, with intermittent blurred vision and marked fatigue. She had several minutes of slurred speech that resolved before arrival; nausea persists without vomiting. Denies recent injury. She recalls a similar episode of painful visual blurring in one eye several years ago but has no established neurologic diagnosis. History includes diabetes. Her mother has atrial fibrillation. Symptoms have been present intermittently for most of today.

Symptoms: left-sided arm and leg weakness; numbness on the left side; blurred vision; difficulty speaking; fatigue; nausea
Case_History_Text: I am his older sister, and I met him at the emergency department after a neighbor called EMS. He is 24 and works as a home health aide. About two hours before arriving, he called the neighbor because his left hand felt numb and his left leg became unsteady. The neighbor noticed that his speech sounded slowed and that he kept rubbing his eyes, saying the vision on one side looked blurred. He was awake and understood questions but had trouble getting some words out. He also felt nauseated and unusually tired. He has mentioned becoming drained during hot weather before, but he has never had symptoms this noticeable. He has no known history of similar episodes, and the neighbor brought his phone and work bag with him.

Symptoms: left-sided arm and leg weakness; tingling on the left side; blurred vision; brief slurred speech; trouble keeping balance; fatigue
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am 27 and work on a farm. About six hours ago, while working with a coworker, I noticed tingling and weakness affecting my left hand and leg. My vision became blurred in one eye, and I felt unsteady when walking. I also had a few minutes of slurred speech, which has improved, but the weakness and altered sensation have continued. I feel unusually tired and have had trouble keeping my balance. Several years ago I had an episode of painful vision changes that resolved, and I have had a couple of shorter spells of tingling and clumsiness since then, though I was never given a definite explanation. My coworker brought me to the emergency department because this episode feels more persistent.

Symptoms: left arm numbness and weakness; blurred vision; brief slurred speech; fatigue; symptoms fluctuating over three hours
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: Forty-year-old man, a restaurant cook, brought from work with a coworker after EMS was called for approximately three hours of intermittent left arm numbness and weakness. He reports blurred vision that began while preparing food and says his speech sounded slurred for several minutes before improving. He describes marked fatigue and recalls similar vision trouble in one eye several years ago, though he has never received a specific neurologic diagnosis. He denies known heart disease but reports that his father has atrial fibrillation. Symptoms have varied in intensity during transport.

Symptoms: left-sided arm numbness and weakness; blurred vision in the left eye; difficulty finding words; unsteady balance; sudden onset 45 minutes ago
Case_History_Text: A 37-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by a former coworker after developing sudden neurologic symptoms approximately 45 minutes before arrival. She first noticed tingling and clumsiness in her left hand while sitting at home, followed by a sense that her left leg was not moving normally when she stood. Her coworker reports that she appeared unsteady and had difficulty getting words out, although she remained able to answer questions. The patient describes blurred vision affecting the left side of her vision without eye pain and says the left arm now feels numb and heavy. She denies fainting, chest discomfort, severe headache, recent head injury, or witnessed seizure-like activity. She has no known prior neurologic diagnosis. She reports several months of pronounced fatigue and occasional worsening of her balance during hot weather. She is currently unemployed and lives alone. No recent illness or medication change is reported.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: A 55-year-old woman, employed as an office administrator, arrived alone to the emergency department for abdominal pain that began approximately 45 minutes ago. She describes intermittent cramping centered around the mid-abdomen, with discomfort that has become more noticeable since onset. Nausea developed shortly afterward, followed by two episodes of nonbloody vomiting. She also reports one loose stool earlier this evening but denies seeing blood. She has not identified a clear food trigger and is unsure whether movement changes the discomfort. She reports feeling generally uncomfortable but denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or urinary symptoms. She has had no recent travel or known sick contacts. Her medical history is otherwise unremarkable by her account, and she takes no regular prescription medications. She drinks alcohol socially, usually on weekends. She appears worried and asks whether she may have eaten something that did not agree with her.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; belching; constipation
Case_History_Text: I’m 66 and work as a high school coach. Since yesterday, I’ve had cramping pain across my abdomen that comes and goes, along with nausea and several episodes of vomiting. I’ve been belching more than usual and feel unusually full and uncomfortable. I haven’t had a bowel movement since yesterday morning, which is not typical for me, though I have passed a little gas. I tried sipping water but vomited again. I have not noticed a fever or blood in the vomit. I had abdominal surgery many years ago, but I’ve generally been well since then. I drink alcohol on some weekends. My adult daughter called EMS because the pain and vomiting worsened tonight, and she came with me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; diarrhea; belching; bloating
Case_History_Text: Triage note: 36-y/o woman, software engineer, arrives to ED with neighbor for abdominal pain since last night. Reports diffuse cramping with bloating and frequent belching, followed by nausea and several episodes of vomiting. Also notes loose stools, without reported blood. No prior abdominal surgery. States she drinks alcohol on some weekends and uses NSAIDs for chronic joint pain. Remote episodes of right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals, not recently evaluated. Appears uncomfortable but conversant; symptoms began after an ordinary evening meal. No additional concerns reported at triage.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting
Case_History_Text: I am his sister, and I came to the emergency department after his coworker called EMS from the construction site. He is 68 and works as a construction foreman. He said his stomach had been hurting on and off since yesterday evening, but this morning the discomfort became more noticeable and he began vomiting several times. He has continued to feel nauseated and has had little interest in food or fluids. He often uses antacids for recurring indigestion, though he has not reported this kind of episode before. He could not identify a particular meal or injury that started it. Between episodes, he seems tired but alert and answers questions appropriately.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: I am a 67-year-old woman who came to the emergency department with my neighbor because I have felt increasingly unwell since this morning. I developed cramping abdominal pain that comes in waves, along with nausea and several episodes of vomiting. I have also had loose stools, though not much has passed since the pain became worse. I feel bloated and weak and have been unable to keep down food or much water. I work as a security guard and had to leave my shift early. I sometimes have “irritable bowels,” according to my own description, and take over-the-counter NSAIDs for chronic joint pain. I have not had prior abdominal surgery. The pain is still present, and I would like to be evaluated.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; feverish feeling; diarrhea; constipation
Case_History_Text: EMS reports a 56-year-old man brought to the emergency department with his neighbor after EMS was called for approximately two hours of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and repeated vomiting. He describes the pain as crampy and centered around the mid-abdomen, with intermittent waves of increased discomfort. He felt feverish but did not measure his temperature. He reports one loose stool earlier today, followed by difficulty passing stool and gas. His history includes abdominal surgery several years ago and frequent use of over-the-counter antacids. He is a rideshare driver and was at home when symptoms intensified.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; bloating
Case_History_Text: A 66-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with her adult daughter for approximately six hours of abdominal discomfort, nausea, and repeated vomiting. She describes the pain as initially centered around the mid-abdomen and now more diffuse, coming in waves with a persistent dull component between episodes. She reports increasing bloating and says that eating or drinking worsens the nausea. The emesis has been nonbloody, without unusual color, and she has not noticed fever, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath. She denies recent abdominal injury. She has never required abdominal surgery. Her daughter reports that the patient was well earlier in the day and became uncomfortable during an afternoon class. The patient is a college student and remains independent with daily activities. She recalls having intermittent right-upper-abdominal pain after fatty meals several years ago, but says that those episodes resolved and felt different from today’s symptoms. She has not experienced this combination of pain, bloating, and vomiting recently.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; loss of appetite; bloating; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I’m 59 and work as a warehouse supervisor. About three hours ago, I developed cramping pain across the middle of my abdomen, followed by nausea and several episodes of vomiting. My belly feels bloated, and I have not wanted to eat since this started. I’ve felt a little feverish, but I did not check my temperature. My wife called EMS because the pain kept coming back and I looked pale. She came with me to the emergency department. Years ago, I sometimes had pain under my right ribs after eating greasy foods, but that had not bothered me recently. I had an abdominal operation many years ago for a hernia. I do not recall any recent injury, unusual meal, or illness in the family.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; belching; diarrhea; bloating; decreased appetite
Case_History_Text: 53F warehouse supervisor brought to ED by coworker for sudden-onset crampy abdominal discomfort beginning 45 min ago, with nausea and two episodes of nonbloody emesis. Reports frequent belching, abdominal bloating, and little appetite today. Also had one loose stool earlier; denies blood. Pain is poorly localized and comes in waves. Uses ibuprofen intermittently for chronic joint pain and drinks alcohol on weekends. No prior abdominal surgery reported. Appears uncomfortable but conversant; no additional history available at triage.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; bloating
Case_History_Text: I brought my 53-year-old father to the emergency department after calling EMS this afternoon. He has had cramping abdominal pain since yesterday, mostly around the middle of his abdomen, with increasing bloating. He became nauseated and has vomited several times, bringing up mostly food and later small amounts of fluid. He says the discomfort comes in waves, though he has not been able to get comfortable. He drives a city bus and tried to rest between shifts, but the symptoms worsened overnight. He had abdominal surgery many years ago, although he has otherwise been fairly well. He denies a recent injury or known sick contact. He looked tired and uncomfortable during the ride, but remained alert and able to answer questions.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; loose stool followed by constipation; poor oral intake
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 32-year-old woman and a construction foreman. I came to the emergency department with a coworker because abdominal pain began last night and has steadily worsened. The pain is crampy across the middle of my abdomen, with bloating and waves of nausea. I have vomited several times since early this morning and have barely been able to keep down water. I had one loose stool overnight but have not had another bowel movement today and feel uncomfortable and full. I use antacids fairly often for indigestion, but this feels different. I have not had any abdominal operations. My coworker says I look pale and tired, though I have not fainted or had chest pain.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; reduced appetite; intermittent diarrhea; constipation; subjective low-grade feverish feeling; poor oral intake
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 75-year-old man, a retired nurse, brought from home with his spouse after she called for help. He reports cramping abdominal pain that has come and gone since yesterday evening, with nausea and several episodes of vomiting. He has had little to eat or drink, feels feverish, and describes loose stool earlier but no bowel movement since, with increasing constipation. His spouse says he has been less active today. He drinks alcohol on some weekends. He has a history of remote abdominal surgery, though the details are not immediately available. No 12-lead interpretation provided.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by a coworker after developing abdominal discomfort during her security shift earlier today. She describes the pain as cramping and centered around the mid-abdomen, coming in waves and becoming more persistent over the last several hours. Nausea began soon afterward, followed by several episodes of nonbloody vomiting that have limited her ability to keep down fluids. She reports feeling feverish but has not measured her temperature. She recalls passing a small amount of stool this morning and is unsure whether she has passed gas since the pain began. She denies known exposure to anyone ill and has not identified a specific food trigger. By self-report, she has irritable bowels with occasional prior episodes of abdominal cramping, though she says today’s symptoms feel more intense. She has no other acute complaints and is alert but uncomfortable during the interview.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; bloating; loss of appetite; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: I’m a 74-year-old man and work as an office administrator. About two hours ago, I developed cramping pain across my abdomen, followed by nausea and several episodes of vomiting. My belly feels unusually bloated, and I have not wanted to eat. I’ve also had loose stools since this started. I barely ate or drank much today because I felt uncomfortable. My wife became worried when the pain and vomiting continued, so she called EMS, and they brought me to the emergency department. I usually have a couple of drinks on weekends but do not drink every day. I have not had any recent operations. I’m feeling weak and thirsty, but I have not noticed anything else unusual.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; constipation; diarrhea; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: 40-year-old woman, warehouse supervisor, arrived to ED with coworker. Reports roughly 6 hrs of worsening crampy abdominal pain, mainly central, with nausea and several episodes of vomiting. Appetite decreased. States she has not had a normal bowel movement today but had one loose stool earlier. Denies prior abdominal surgery. Notes similar right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals several years ago, now resolved. Drinks alcohol on some weekends. Appears uncomfortable but able to answer questions; no additional history available at triage.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; constipation; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I brought my 28-year-old brother to the emergency department after his coworker called EMS from the bus depot. He drives a city bus and had been working normally until about three hours ago, when he developed cramping abdominal pain that gradually became difficult for him to ignore. He has vomited several times and says he feels nauseated even between episodes. He has not had a bowel movement today, which is unusual enough for him to mention, though he often describes himself as having “irritable bowels.” He also feels feverish but has not checked his temperature. During the ride here he looked uncomfortable, shifted constantly in his seat, and could only take small sips of water. He has no known recent injury and came in wearing his work uniform.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; bloating; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 52-year-old woman who came to the emergency department with my coworker from the daycare where I work. About 45 minutes ago, I developed worsening abdominal pain with a bloated, tight feeling. I have vomited several times and still feel very nauseated. I have not wanted to eat today and have had very little to drink. The pain is not clearly relieved by changing position. Years ago, I sometimes had discomfort under my right ribs after fatty meals, but I have not had this kind of episode recently. I have not had abdominal surgery. I feel weak and uncomfortable and would like to be evaluated.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; diarrhea; belching; low-grade feverish feeling; decreased oral intake
Case_History_Text: EMS brought a 46-year-old man to the emergency department after his adult daughter called for help. He reports about one day of crampy, intermittent abdominal pain with nausea and several episodes of vomiting. He has also had loose stools, frequent belching, and a low-grade feverish feeling without a measured temperature. He says he has barely eaten or drank since yesterday. The patient describes a history of “irritable bowels” by self-report and works as a librarian. He denies regular alcohol use but drinks on some weekends. He remained alert and conversational during transport.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; constipation; belching
Case_History_Text: A 43-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with her spouse for abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting that began last night. She describes the pain as cramping and mostly central, occurring in waves and becoming more uncomfortable this morning. She has vomited several times, initially food contents and later small amounts of clear fluid. She reports increased belching and says her abdomen feels fuller than usual. Her last bowel movement was yesterday morning, and she has not passed much gas since then, though she notes that her bowel pattern can vary. She denies knowing of any unusual foods or sick contacts and has not noticed blood in the vomit or stool. She reports a history of “irritable bowels” by self-report but no prior episode quite like this. She works as a nurse and tried sipping water at home without relief. Her spouse drove her to the department after the pain and vomiting continued overnight.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; intermittent diarrhea and constipation; poor oral intake
Case_History_Text: I’m 55 and work as an accountant. The stomach pain started on and off yesterday evening and has become harder to ignore today. It feels crampy across my abdomen, with periods when it eases and then returns. I’ve been nauseated and have vomited several times, mostly liquid because I have barely been able to eat or drink. I had a loose stool earlier, but since then I haven’t been able to pass much stool. I feel bloated and tired, without any known fever. A coworker stayed with me and called EMS when I became lightheaded while standing. EMS brought me to the emergency department, and my coworker is here with me. I have not had abdominal surgery before.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; constipation; belching; loose stool
Case_History_Text: 55F, welder, arrived to ED with spouse for diffuse crampy abdominal pain beginning this morning, gradually worsening. Reports nausea with 3 episodes of nonbloody emesis, frequent belching, and feeling constipated; had one small loose stool earlier today. Denies known fever, chest pain, or urinary symptoms. States similar right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals years ago, but no recent episodes. Takes ibuprofen regularly for joint pain. No prior abdominal operations reported. Appears uncomfortable but alert and speaking clearly. Triage vitals nonconcerning.
Model_Diagnosis: Gallstone ileus causing small bowel obstruction

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; feeling feverish; poor oral intake
Case_History_Text: I brought my 28-year-old son to the emergency department after calling EMS from our farm this evening. He had been working outdoors earlier and seemed well until about two hours ago, when he developed cramping abdominal pain that came in waves. He became nauseated and vomited several times, mostly fluid and recently eaten food. He says his stomach feels unsettled and that he has a low-grade feverish feeling, though he has not measured his temperature. He has taken very little by mouth since the discomfort began because drinking made the nausea worse. Between episodes he is tired and uncomfortable but able to answer questions clearly. He has no known ongoing medical problems that we are aware of, and this is the first time I have seen him this ill.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; bloating; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 44-year-old woman and an accountant. About six hours ago, I developed cramping abdominal pain that has gradually become more persistent, along with noticeable bloating. I have vomited several times and still feel nauseated. I also feel mildly feverish, although I have not checked my temperature at home. My spouse is bringing me to the emergency department because the discomfort and vomiting are not settling. I had abdominal surgery years ago, with no recent procedures. I have also occasionally had right-upper-abdominal discomfort after fatty meals in the past, but this feels more widespread and is accompanied by the bloating and repeated vomiting. I have not had similar symptoms this severe before.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute small bowel obstruction due to postoperative adhesions

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; low-grade feverish feeling; belching; constipation
Case_History_Text: EMS brings a 39-year-old man from home to the emergency department with his spouse after three hours of worsening, crampy abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. He reports feeling feverish, frequent belching, and no bowel movement today, though he is unsure when he last passed gas. He denies chest discomfort or fainting. His spouse says he became pale and sweaty during one episode. He takes over-the-counter NSAIDs several times a week for joint pain and recalls brief right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals years ago. He had a remote abdominal operation, with no recent procedures or injuries. He is alert and able to answer questions.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: A 68-year-old woman, an office administrator, presents to the emergency department with her adult daughter for abdominal pain that began approximately 45 minutes ago. She describes a cramping discomfort centered around the mid-abdomen, occurring in waves and becoming more noticeable over the past half hour. She has felt nauseated and has vomited twice, bringing up recently eaten food without visible blood. She reports little interest in eating since the symptoms began and has not tried any medication before arrival. She denies chest discomfort, shortness of breath, fainting, or urinary burning. Her daughter says the patient appeared uncomfortable while traveling to the hospital but remained alert and able to walk with assistance. The patient recalls a remote abdominal operation many years ago but is unsure of the specific details and has had no recent procedures. She reports no known sick contacts and no recent change in her usual bowel habits. She is concerned because the pain and vomiting started abruptly.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a coworker from her nursing unit for abdominal pain that began approximately 45 minutes ago. She describes the discomfort as cramping and centered around the mid-abdomen, with occasional aching toward the lower abdomen, without a clear precipitating event. She has vomited twice since the pain started and continues to feel nauseated. She reports having little interest in food today but denies eating anything unusual before symptoms began. She is unsure whether movement changes the pain and has not noticed a consistent relationship to bowel movements. She denies known recent injury and has not had similar symptoms recently. Her coworker says she appeared uncomfortable during their shift and asked to leave early. The patient takes over-the-counter NSAIDs intermittently for chronic joint pain, with the last dose several days ago. No other medication or medical history is provided at triage.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; belching
Case_History_Text: I’m 45 and work as an office administrator. My spouse called EMS tonight because the abdominal pain I’ve had since yesterday became harder to ignore. It started as a vague cramping feeling around the middle of my belly and now feels more constant, though I can’t point to one exact spot. I’ve been nauseated and have vomited several times, mostly after trying to drink water. I keep belching and feel bloated. I haven’t wanted food today. Years ago, I sometimes had pain high on the right side after fatty meals, but this feels different. I call myself someone with irritable bowels because my stools can be unpredictable. I’m not aware of any recent injury or unusual food, and I came to the emergency department with my spouse.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; bloating; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: 34-y/o woman, restaurant cook, brought to ED by neighbor for abd pain since last night. Pain began as diffuse cramping with bloating and has remained mostly around the mid-abdomen, intermittently worse with movement. Reports nausea, 4 episodes of nonbloody emesis, and several loose stools. Denies known fever, chest pain, or urinary complaints. PMH notable for occasional right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals years ago. Uses NSAIDs intermittently for joint pain. Drinks alcohol on weekends. Appears uncomfortable but conversant at triage.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; constipation; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I brought my husband to the emergency department after calling EMS because his stomach pain kept returning and became harder for him to ignore. He is 27 and works as a construction foreman. The discomfort started yesterday evening around his mid-abdomen and has come and gone, sometimes spreading more generally across his belly. He has felt nauseated and vomited several times since last night. He says he has not had a normal bowel movement since yesterday and feels mildly feverish, though we did not check his temperature at home. He has been taking over-the-counter NSAIDs for recurring joint pain at work. Until today he was still trying to manage things himself, but this afternoon he became pale, tired, and unable to keep fluids down.

Symptoms: abdominal pain; nausea; vomiting; loose stools; constipation
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m writing about my mother, who asked me to explain what has been happening since we arrived at the emergency department. She is 26 and manages a retail store. For most of today she has had cramping abdominal pain, initially around the middle of her abdomen and now more noticeable across the lower abdomen, though it comes and goes. Symptoms: LLQ abdominal pain x45 min; bloating; diarrhea; vomiting; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: 71-year-old woman, retired accountant, brought to ED by a neighbor for sudden worsening LLQ abdominal pain over the past 45 min. Reports abdominal bloating, several loose stools, one episode of vomiting, and feeling feverish with a low-grade temperature at home. Denies recent trauma. PMH notable for prior abdominal surgery. Uses antacids frequently and drinks alcohol on weekends. Appears uncomfortable but conversant at triage; no acute change in mental status reported. Neighbor states symptoms began while patient was resting at home.

Symptoms: left lower abdominal pain for one day; low-grade feverish feeling; bloating; reduced appetite; discomfort worse with movement
Case_History_Text: I brought my coworker, a 61-year-old man who coaches at the local high school, to the emergency department after we called EMS this evening. He had been complaining since yesterday of steady pain in the lower left side of his abdomen, which became more noticeable after dinner and has made walking upright uncomfortable. He says he feels feverish but has not measured his temperature. His abdomen feels bloated, and he has eaten very little today. He has not mentioned chest discomfort or trouble breathing. He seemed tired and quieter than usual, though he was able to answer questions clearly. He usually functions independently and is active at school. He drinks alcohol on some weekends but does not regularly discuss other health problems.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain since last night; low-grade fever; vomiting; bloating; constipation
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am writing for my mother, a 53-year-old woman who came to the emergency department with me today. She developed aching pain in the lower left side of her abdomen last night, and it has become more persistent since then. She says her abdomen feels bloated and she has not had a bowel movement since yesterday. She vomited twice this morning and has been able to drink only small sips. At home her temperature was slightly elevated. She does not describe chest discomfort or trouble breathing. She is currently unemployed and drinks alcohol most weekends. Her last screening colonoscopy was several years ago, but we do not have the report available. She has not had this exact combination of symptoms before.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; intermittent diarrhea; recent constipation; bloating; belching
Case_History_Text: EMS reports a 73-year-old man brought from his retail store after a coworker called for help. He describes left lower-quadrant abdominal pain that began on and off yesterday evening and has become more persistent today, with bloating, belching, and alternating constipation and loose stools. He feels feverish; oral temperature was 100.8°F, with otherwise stable, non-distressed vital signs. He denies chest discomfort and reports no recent injury. He says he has “irritable bowels,” uses ibuprofen frequently for joint pain, and had episodes of right-upper-abdominal discomfort after fatty meals several years ago. He is alert and able to provide the history.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; loose stools; decreased appetite; abdominal tenderness
Case_History_Text: A 63-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by a neighbor for abdominal pain that began earlier today and gradually became more persistent. She describes the discomfort as centered in the left lower abdomen, initially cramping but now more constant, with occasional sharper twinges when walking or changing position. She reports several loose stools since morning without visible blood and has had little interest in food. She noticed feeling warm at home but denies shaking chills. She has not vomited and is able to sip fluids. She denies chest discomfort, shortness of breath, dysuria, or flank pain. The patient works at a daycare and wondered whether she had picked up a stomach illness, although no coworkers are known to be ill. She takes over-the-counter naproxen intermittently for chronic knee and hand joint pain, with the last dose yesterday evening. Her neighbor reports that she appeared uncomfortable but was alert and walking independently before arrival.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; nausea; vomiting; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: I’m 61 and work as a warehouse supervisor. About two hours ago, I developed a steady aching pain on the lower left side of my abdomen that has become intense enough that I had to stop moving around. I felt feverish and nauseated, then vomited once and had several loose stools. My wife became worried when I looked pale and called EMS, and she came with me to the emergency department. I have not had pain like this before. I drink alcohol mostly on weekends. Several years ago, I sometimes had pain under the right side of my ribs after greasy meals, but that went away and has not bothered me recently. The abdominal pain is still present and worse when I try to sit upright.

Symptoms: LLQ abdominal pain x6 hr; bloating; constipation; belching; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: 73F brought to ED by spouse for approx 6 hr of worsening LLQ abdominal pain with bloating and no bowel movement today. Reports increased belching and feeling feverish; denies vomiting. Appears uncomfortable but ambulatory. Temp 100.4°F at triage. PMH notable for frequent antacid use and weekend alcohol intake. States she had intermittent right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals several years ago, not recently. Works as a janitor. Spouse reports pain has limited her usual activity this evening.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain for three hours; low-grade feverish feeling; decreased appetite; constipation; increasing abdominal tenderness
Case_History_Text: I brought my 70-year-old coworker to the emergency department after calling EMS because his lower abdominal pain became much worse over the last three hours. He points to the left lower side and says it has stayed in one area, though movement makes it more uncomfortable. He feels feverish, and the crew noted a low-grade temperature on arrival. He has not wanted to eat since the pain began and says he has been constipated recently, with less frequent bowel movements than usual. He is a retired nurse and initially thought he could rest at home, but he became pale and uncomfortable while we were together. He has not mentioned chest pain or trouble breathing, and he has had no recent abdominal injury.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; constipation; vomiting; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 73-year-old woman who came to the emergency department with my daughter. About 45 minutes ago, I developed steady pain on the lower left side of my abdomen. It has become difficult to ignore and feels worse when I shift position. I have felt feverish, and my daughter says I seem flushed. I have not had a bowel movement today and have passed very little gas. I vomited once on the way here and have no appetite. My medical history includes abdominal surgery many years ago. I also used to have occasional right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals, though that has not bothered me recently. I work part-time as a graphic designer and was otherwise functioning normally before this started.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute small bowel obstruction due to postoperative adhesions

Symptoms: left lower quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; nausea; constipation; bloating; decreased appetite
Case_History_Text: EMS brought a 71-year-old man from home to the emergency department after his neighbor called for help. He reports about one day of worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain, with bloating, nausea, little appetite, and no bowel movement since yesterday. He describes the pain as persistent and severe enough that he has had difficulty resting. He felt chilled but denies fainting or chest discomfort. He is a retired postal worker, drinks alcohol on some weekends, and has a history of constipation. He recalls a screening colonoscopy several years ago. On arrival, he was alert and speaking clearly, with a low-grade fever and otherwise stable-appearing vital signs.

Symptoms: left lower quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade feverish feeling; belching; reduced appetite
Case_History_Text: A 60-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with her spouse for left lower quadrant abdominal pain that began last night after dinner. She describes the discomfort as steady, cramping, and gradually more bothersome through the morning, with occasional sharper waves when she moves or changes position. She reports feeling feverish but has not measured a high temperature. She has been belching more than usual and has eaten very little today because food seems unappealing. She denies vomiting and says her bowel movements have been less comfortable than usual, though she has not noticed obvious blood. She reports no recent travel or known sick contacts. The patient works as a restaurant cook and initially tried to continue her shift, but the pain became distracting. Her spouse encouraged her to seek care when she appeared flushed and uncomfortable. She regularly uses over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medication for chronic joint pain but has not taken anything for this episode. She has no prior similar episode documented in the available history.

Symptoms: left lower abdominal pain; low-grade feverish feeling; intermittent diarrhea; vomiting; nausea; abdominal tenderness
Case_History_Text: I’m 74 and work at a daycare. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had pain on and off in the lower left side of my abdomen. It became more uncomfortable this morning, so my spouse called EMS and came with me to the emergency department. I’ve felt feverish but not intensely hot, and I’ve had several loose stools with two episodes of vomiting. I’m nauseated and have not wanted much to eat or drink. The pain seems worse when I move around, though I can still speak normally and walk with help. I had abdominal surgery years ago, but I don’t remember any recent problems from it. I use antacids frequently for recurring indigestion and take no new medicines.

Symptoms: LLQ abdominal pain; low-grade fever; poor appetite; constipation; bloating; vomiting
Case_History_Text: 77-year-old woman, retired teacher, arrived alone to ED. Reports LLQ abdominal pain beginning earlier today, gradually worsening and persistent. Also notes feeling feverish, decreased appetite, constipation, and abdominal bloating. Vomited twice this afternoon, nonbloody. Denies recent injury. Triage temp 100.4°F; otherwise initial vital signs stable. History includes prior abdominal surgery, frequent antacid use, and alcohol on weekends. No medication list available at triage. Patient appears uncomfortable but is speaking clearly and ambulatory. Awaiting further evaluation.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; vomiting; abdominal bloating; worsening tenderness with movement
Case_History_Text: I am his sister, and I met him in the emergency department after a neighbor called EMS and rode with him. He is 67 and works as a nurse, usually active and independent. About two hours before arrival, he developed aching pain in the lower left side of his abdomen that became more constant and severe. He said his abdomen felt swollen and that moving or riding in the ambulance made the pain worse. He vomited twice but denied passing out or having chest discomfort. The neighbor said he looked flushed and felt warm. He occasionally drinks several beers on weekends but has no known recent injury or unusual meal. He seemed uncomfortable, tired, and worried, though he answered questions appropriately.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; nausea; bloating; constipation
Case_History_Text: I am a 61-year-old accountant and came to the emergency department alone because of worsening pain on the lower left side of my abdomen. It began about six hours ago and has become fairly constant, with occasional sharper waves when I move. I feel bloated and nauseated but have not vomited. I have been constipated today and have not passed much stool. At home I measured a low-grade fever. I take ibuprofen several times a week for joint pain and usually drink a few alcoholic beverages on weekends. I do not recall eating anything unusual or having a recent injury. I am normally independent and had been working earlier today, but the discomfort now makes it difficult to sit comfortably.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain; low-grade fever; bloating; belching; diarrhea; vomiting
Case_History_Text: EMS brings a 45-year-old man from home after his neighbor called for help. He reports three hours of progressively worsening left lower-quadrant abdominal pain with bloating and frequent belching. He had several loose stools and vomited once before our arrival, and he felt warm at home. He denies chest discomfort, fainting, or recent injury. He coaches at a high school and says he has used over-the-counter NSAIDs for recurring joint pain. He recalls a screening colonoscopy several years ago and remote episodes of right-upper-abdominal discomfort after fatty meals, but no similar recent illness. He arrives alert, uncomfortable, and speaking clearly.

Symptoms: left lower-quadrant abdominal pain for 45 minutes; low-grade feverish feeling; constipation; abdominal tenderness
Case_History_Text: A 46-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by a neighbor for sudden-onset left lower-quadrant abdominal pain that began approximately 45 minutes ago. She describes the discomfort as steady and deep, with intermittent sharper waves, and rates it 8/10. She reports feeling mildly feverish but has not measured her temperature. She has been constipated recently, with her last bowel movement yesterday and increased straining today. She denies vomiting, diarrhea, urinary burning, visible blood in the urine, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath. She has not had a similar episode in this location. The pain has made it difficult for her to walk comfortably, though she remains able to answer questions clearly. She works as a home health aide and was at home preparing for work when symptoms started. She recalls episodes of right-upper-belly discomfort after fatty meals several years ago but has had no recent symptoms there. No prior abdominal operations are reported.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; decreased appetite; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: A 63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her adult daughter for approximately 45 minutes of persistent epigastric pain. She describes the discomfort as a pressure-like ache in the upper central abdomen without a clear relationship to meals and says it has remained fairly constant since it began while she was preparing for work. Nausea followed shortly afterward, with two episodes of nonbloody vomiting. She also reports feeling unusually fatigued and has had little appetite today. She mentions one loose stool earlier in the morning but denies blood or black discoloration. She has not noticed fever, chills, shortness of breath, fainting, or palpitations. The patient works as a warehouse supervisor and states she felt generally well before this episode. She drinks alcohol socially, usually on weekends, but denies drinking today. Her daughter says the patient appeared pale and uncomfortable at home, prompting the visit. No similar recent episode is reported.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome (inferior-wall myocardial infarction presenting as epigastric pain)

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; loss of appetite; bloating; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I’m 44 and work as a construction foreman. Since yesterday, I’ve had a dull, uncomfortable pain high in my stomach that comes and goes, with a bloated feeling. I’ve been nauseated and vomited several times, mostly after trying to eat, and I haven’t had much appetite. I also feel unusually tired and a little feverish, though I haven’t checked my temperature. I took some over-the-counter medicine for my aching joints yesterday, as I do fairly often, but it didn’t help this pain. I have diabetes and take my usual medications. My adult daughter called EMS because I looked pale and weak at home, and she came with me to the emergency department. I deny any recent injury.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; bloating; constipation
Case_History_Text: 72-y/o woman, construction foreman, brought to ED by neighbor for epigastric discomfort beginning last night. Reports persistent nausea with several episodes of vomiting, marked fatigue, belching, and abdominal bloating. States she has not had a bowel movement recently. Denies known injury. Uses antacids frequently for recurrent upper abdominal burning. Drinks alcohol on weekends. PMH notable for prior abdominal surgery; details unavailable at triage. Appears uncomfortable but cooperative. Neighbor reports she seemed more tired than usual this morning. Further history limited by ongoing nausea.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; intermittent discomfort; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I am his sister, and I spoke with EMS before they brought my 52-year-old brother to the emergency department. He is a pharmacist and usually keeps working through minor illnesses, but he has had episodes of aching and pressure in the upper abdomen on and off since yesterday evening. He became nauseated, vomited several times, and says he feels unusually tired and feverish. He has not described a sharp pain or a clear connection to meals, though he has been uncomfortable enough to stop eating. A neighbor stayed with him and accompanied him after EMS was called. He reports having “irritable bowels” in the past but no similar episode this intense. He has not mentioned any other new symptoms, and the neighbor says he looked pale and worn out before transport.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; bloating
Case_History_Text: I am a 55-year-old accountant who came to the emergency department with my daughter because I have felt unwell for most of today. The discomfort is centered high in my abdomen and feels like a steady pressure with occasional cramping. I have been bloated, nauseated, and have vomited twice, without noticing blood. I feel unusually tired and mildly clammy, though I have not checked my temperature. I sometimes have indigestion after meals and have called my bowels irritable in the past, but this episode feels more persistent than usual. I do not recall a specific food trigger. My daughter says I look pale, and I would like to be evaluated.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; bloating; constipation
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We were called to the patient’s home for a 41-year-old man with about two hours of persistent upper abdominal discomfort. He points to the epigastric area and describes pressure with bloating, accompanied by nausea and two episodes of vomiting. His spouse reports that he appeared unusually tired and encouraged him to seek care. He works as a home health aide and has been using antacids frequently for intermittent indigestion. He reports constipation today. He had abdominal surgery several years ago and recalls episodes of right-upper-abdominal pain after fatty meals in the distant past. He arrives in the ED with his spouse for further evaluation.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; diarrhea; bloating
Case_History_Text: A 43-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by her adult daughter for approximately six hours of persistent upper abdominal discomfort. She describes a pressure-like ache centered in the epigastrium, initially intermittent but now more constant, without a clear positional trigger. She has had several episodes of nonbloody vomiting and two loose stools since the pain began, along with marked fatigue and abdominal bloating. She denies a measured fever and has not noticed visible blood in the stool or vomitus. She reports occasional indigestion after meals over the past year, usually relieved with over-the-counter remedies, but says this episode is more prolonged and intense than usual. She has had little oral intake today. She works as a city bus driver and recalls feeling generally run down during her shift before symptoms became prominent. Her daughter notes that she appeared pale and uncomfortable at home. No additional history is available at triage.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; bloating; constipation
Case_History_Text: I’m 65 and drive for a rideshare service. About three hours ago, while I was sitting at home after finishing a shift, I developed a steady aching pain high in my abdomen. It feels like pressure and has made me nauseated. I’ve vomited twice, mostly food and liquid, and feel unusually tired and weak. My belly also feels bloated, and I have not had a bowel movement today, though I sometimes get constipated. I don’t really notice the pain elsewhere, and I haven’t had this exact feeling before. I drink alcohol on some weekends. For my joint pain, I take over-the-counter anti-inflammatory pills several days a week. My neighbor became concerned when I looked pale and called EMS, who brought me here.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; bloating; diarrhea
Case_History_Text: 57-year-old woman, auto mechanic, arrives to ED with adult daughter for 45 min of sudden upper abdominal/epigastric pressure and queasiness. Reports bloating, one episode of vomiting, and loose stool, with unusual fatigue. Says she has had intermittent indigestion after meals and describes a history of “irritable bowels.” She has diabetes. Pain is persistent and difficult for her to characterize; no clear food or activity trigger identified. Daughter states patient appeared pale and rested in the car before arrival. Triage initiated; patient seated upright and awaiting further evaluation.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue
Case_History_Text: I brought my 70-year-old neighbor to the emergency department after calling EMS this morning. He is a retired teacher who lives alone and had been feeling unusually tired since yesterday. Over the past day, he developed a steady ache high in his abdomen, mostly in the middle, with waves of nausea and several episodes of vomiting. He said the discomfort was uncomfortable rather than sharp and had trouble getting comfortable in his recliner. He has not wanted breakfast or dinner and seemed pale and quieter than usual. Years ago, he sometimes complained of pain under the right ribs after eating fried or fatty meals, but this feels more central to him. He has not mentioned a recent injury or illness.

Symptoms: Epigastric pain; nausea; repeated vomiting; fatigue; feverish feeling; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: I am a 79-year-old woman and came to the emergency department with my spouse because of pain high in my abdomen that began last night. It feels like a steady pressure in the middle, with occasional discomfort toward my back, rather than sharp pain. I have been nauseated and have vomited several times, and I feel unusually weak and tired. I have not wanted to eat and feel slightly feverish, though I have not measured a high temperature. I use antacids often for indigestion. Years ago, I sometimes had pain under the right ribs after fatty meals, but this feels more central and persistent. I work as a warehouse supervisor and had to leave early because I felt too drained to continue.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; intermittent diarrhea and constipation
Case_History_Text: EMS brings a 70-year-old man from home to the emergency department after his neighbor called for help. He reports epigastric discomfort that has come and gone since yesterday evening, accompanied by nausea, two episodes of vomiting, belching, and marked fatigue. He also describes irregular bowels, with loose stool earlier and a feeling of constipation today. He is a retired accountant and says he frequently uses antacids for recurrent stomach upset and takes over-the-counter NSAIDs for joint pain. He reports having irritable bowels by self-report. He is alert, speaking clearly, and appears tired but not distressed during transport.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; bloating
Case_History_Text: A 56-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by a neighbor for epigastric discomfort that began earlier today and has persisted for most of the day. She describes the sensation as a deep pressure and burning beneath the breastbone, at times extending slightly toward the lower chest, with intermittent worsening after attempts to eat. She reports repeated nausea and several episodes of nonbloody vomiting, along with frequent belching and a feeling of abdominal fullness. She feels unusually tired and became concerned when the discomfort did not resolve with rest. She denies having had similar prolonged symptoms recently but recalls occasional indigestion. She has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen most days for chronic joint pain, including yesterday and this morning, without food on one occasion. She reports no known recent illness or injury. Her neighbor says she appeared pale and uncomfortable at home, though she remained able to walk to the car.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; constipation; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I’m 50 and coach high school sports. About two hours ago, while getting ready to leave, I developed a steady aching and burning pain high in my abdomen. It has made me nauseated, and I’ve vomited several times without much relief. I feel unusually tired and somewhat feverish, though I haven’t measured my temperature. I have not had a bowel movement today and feel bloated. I don’t really notice pain anywhere else. Years ago, I sometimes had similar right-upper-belly discomfort after eating greasy food, but it had not bothered me recently. I take ibuprofen fairly often for joint pain. My neighbor called EMS and came with me to the emergency department because I looked pale and felt too weak to drive.

Symptoms: Epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; decreased appetite; constipation
Case_History_Text: 45-y/o woman, security guard, arrived alone to ED c/o ~6 hrs of constant epigastric discomfort with nausea and several episodes of emesis. Reports marked fatigue, frequent belching, and poor appetite today. States she has had intermittent indigestion after meals in the past; unsure whether this feels the same. Last bowel movement was yesterday and she feels constipated, though she reports occasional loose stools. Denies recent trauma. PMH includes diabetes. Takes NSAIDs intermittently for chronic joint pain. No medications taken for this episode before arrival.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; loss of appetite; constipation
Case_History_Text: I am his sister and met him in the emergency department after his coworker called EMS from the accounting office. He is a 54-year-old man who had been working when a dull, uncomfortable pain began high in his abdomen about three hours ago. He said it felt worse after trying to eat and became persistent, with nausea followed by two episodes of vomiting. He has looked unusually tired and has not wanted food today. He also mentioned being constipated since yesterday. He often uses over-the-counter antacids for recurring indigestion but said they had not helped this time. He denied any recent injury. His coworker said he appeared pale and was breathing normally while waiting for EMS. He is now resting in a treatment room and answers questions appropriately.

Symptoms: Epigastric pain for 45 minutes; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; loss of appetite; diarrhea; belching
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 58-year-old woman who came to the emergency department with my neighbor because of sudden discomfort high in my abdomen that began about 45 minutes ago. The pain feels like pressure and burning beneath my breastbone and has not fully eased. I have felt nauseated, vomited twice, and become unusually tired and weak. I have also had frequent belching, little interest in food, and one loose stool today. I sometimes get indigestion after meals, but this feels more intense than usual. My medical history includes prior abdominal surgery. I work as a security guard and was on a break when this started. I have not noticed a fever or rash.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; low-grade feverish feeling; belching
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 61-year-old man brought in from his apartment after calling for help because of worsening upper abdominal discomfort over the past day. He describes a steady pressure-like ache in the epigastric area with frequent belching, nausea, and several episodes of vomiting. He reports feeling unusually tired and intermittently feverish but denies knowing of a measured temperature. He arrived alone and is unemployed. He drinks alcohol most weekends, takes over-the-counter NSAIDs for chronic joint pain, and uses antacids frequently. No other history was available during transport.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue
Case_History_Text: A 70-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by a coworker from the postal station for persistent upper abdominal discomfort that began last night after her evening meal. She describes a steady aching and pressure-like sensation centered in the epigastric area, without a clear change with position or movement. The discomfort has continued into today and is accompanied by nausea and several episodes of nonbloody vomiting. She reports feeling unusually tired and had to stop working early because she felt weak. She denies having experienced this exact combination previously. She has not noticed fever, diarrhea, cough, or recent sick contacts. She is unsure whether the discomfort briefly extended toward her lower chest but denies prominent shortness of breath or fainting. Her coworker says she appeared pale and quiet this morning. Her medical history includes diabetes; she is a postal worker and remains physically active on most workdays. Medication adherence and recent dietary changes are not yet clear.

Symptoms: Epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I’m 60 and nonbinary, and I work as a mechanic. This upper-middle stomach pain started yesterday evening, eased up, then returned several times overnight and today. It feels like a deep pressure or burning just below my breastbone, and I’ve been nauseated and vomited a few times. I feel unusually tired and a little feverish, but I haven’t checked my temperature. I used antacids because I take them pretty often for indigestion, though they haven’t helped much this time. Years ago, I sometimes had pain under my right ribs after greasy meals, but this feels more central. My neighbor called EMS and came with me to the emergency department. I’m not sure whether activity changes it, and I haven’t noticed anything else unusual.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; bloating; constipation
Case_History_Text: 45F software engineer arrived to ED with neighbor for most-of-day epigastric discomfort, described as pressure/burning, with intermittent bloating and frequent belching. Nauseated and vomited several times; reports marked fatigue and poor oral intake. States bowel movements have been infrequent today and she has a history of “irritable bowels” by self-report. Uses antacids frequently, with little relief from an extra dose this afternoon. PMH significant for diabetes. Denies known recent sick contacts. Appears uncomfortable but conversant at triage; neighbor reports she seemed unusually tired before arrival.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; bloating; belching
Case_History_Text: I brought my 56-year-old brother to the emergency department after his coworker called EMS from the welding shop. He had been working normally when he developed a pressure-like discomfort high in his abdomen about two hours ago. He became nauseated, vomited several times, and said he felt unusually tired and weak. Before leaving, he complained of bloating and kept belching, which he said briefly eased the discomfort. He has mentioned indigestion after meals for months but has never had pain this persistent. He did not want to come in at first, thinking it was something he ate, but his coworker was concerned when he became pale and quiet. He has no other details available to me.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; bloating; low-grade feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 42-year-old farmer who came to the emergency department with my neighbor. About six hours ago, I developed a steady discomfort high in my abdomen, followed by nausea and several episodes of vomiting. I feel unusually tired and somewhat feverish, although I have not checked my temperature. My stomach feels bloated, and I have been belching more than usual. I sometimes get indigestion after meals, but this episode feels more persistent than normal. I have been taking over-the-counter NSAIDs for ongoing joint pain, including recently. I have not noticed anything else unusual and would appreciate an evaluation, since the discomfort and fatigue have not improved.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; belching; low-grade feverish feeling; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 51-year-old man, a librarian, brought in after his coworker called EMS for three hours of worsening upper abdominal discomfort. He describes the pain as centered in the epigastrium, with persistent nausea, two episodes of vomiting, marked fatigue, belching, and a feverish feeling without a measured temperature. He has had little appetite today. He reports occasional indigestion after meals and recalls episodes of right-upper-belly pain after fatty meals several years ago. History includes diabetes. His coworker says he appeared pale and uncomfortable at work but remained alert and communicative throughout transport.

Symptoms: epigastric pain; nausea; vomiting; fatigue; loss of appetite
Case_History_Text: A 48-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her adult daughter for approximately 45 minutes of sudden epigastric discomfort. She describes the sensation as a deep pressure and burning beneath the upper abdomen, without a clearly identifiable food trigger. The discomfort has remained present and is accompanied by nausea, two episodes of nonbloody vomiting, and marked fatigue. She reports little appetite today and says she felt generally well earlier in the afternoon while driving for work. She denies recent fever, diarrhea, or similar severe episodes, though she has used over-the-counter antacids frequently for intermittent upper-abdominal burning over the past several months. She is unsure whether the antacids have helped consistently. Her daughter noticed that she appeared pale and quiet during the drive to the hospital. The patient denies a recent injury and has no other acute concerns to report.

Symptoms: left flank pain; nausea; one episode of vomiting; restlessness
Case_History_Text: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with her neighbor for abrupt left-sided flank pain that began approximately 45 minutes ago while she was driving for work. She describes the pain as severe, constant, and deep, with intermittent waves of increased intensity that make it difficult for her to remain still. The discomfort has not clearly changed with position. She became nauseated and vomited once before arrival, without blood. She denies recent trauma. She describes intermittent mild lower abdominal cramping without severe or persistent pain. She has had no fainting, chest discomfort, shortness of breath at rest, fever, or recent injury. She takes a prescribed blood thinner for a longstanding heart condition and reports no recent medication changes. She has not knowingly eaten anything unusual and denies vomiting. On arrival, she is alert, conversant, and mildly anxious, with blood pressure and pulse similar to her usual readings. Her coworker says she appeared pale and slower than usual at work this morning.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute gastrointestinal hemorrhage (likely lower GI bleeding) in an anticoagulated patient

Symptoms: Intermittent rectal bleeding or dark stools since yesterday evening; fatigue; mild abdominal cramping; nausea
Case_History_Text: I’m 58 and work on a farm. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had episodes of bleeding when I use the bathroom, and some of the stool looked unusually dark. It has come and gone rather than happening constantly. I feel more tired than usual and a little nauseated, with mild cramping across my abdomen, but no severe pain. I have not passed out or felt confused. I drink alcohol most evenings, and I take over-the-counter ibuprofen daily for aches from farm work. A neighbor called EMS and came with me to the emergency department because I seemed worn out this morning. I’m not sure how much blood there was, but it worried me enough to seek help.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding from NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease

Symptoms: rectal bleeding/melena; fatigue; nausea; lightheadedness when standing; racing heart with walking
Case_History_Text: Triage note: 59F, home health aide, arrived to ED with neighbor for bleeding noticed with bowel movements for most of today. Reports dark red to black-appearing stool and fatigue, with mild nausea. Feels lightheaded on standing and notices her heart racing when walking, improves with rest. Denies fainting or chest discomfort. States she has strained with bowel movements for years. Takes ibuprofen daily for chronic pain and reports regular NSAID use. Awake, speaking clearly, ambulatory with steady assistance. Initial vital signs without marked instability.
Model_Diagnosis: Bleeding peptic ulcer disease (upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage)

Symptoms: rectal bleeding; dark, sticky stool; fatigue; lightheadedness when standing; mild abdominal uneasiness
Case_History_Text: I’m his older sister, and I called EMS when my 33-year-old brother became pale and unsteady at home. He had been feeling unusually tired during his shift as a warehouse supervisor, then about two hours ago noticed dark, sticky stool followed by a small amount of red blood when he wiped. He says he feels lightheaded when standing but has not fainted. He denies severe abdominal pain, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath and has had no recent injury. He arrived alone with EMS, and I met him at the emergency department. He has not had this happen before, though our mother has a chronic liver condition. He is alert and answering questions, but keeps saying he feels drained.

Symptoms: Rectal bleeding or dark stool; fatigue; racing heart with walking; mild abdominal cramping; nausea
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 77-year-old retired mechanic who came to the emergency department with my former coworker. About six hours ago, I noticed unusually dark, sticky stool and a small amount of red blood when wiping. Since then I have felt washed out, with mild cramping across my abdomen and occasional nausea. My heart seems to race when I walk, although I feel steadier sitting down. I have not fainted or had chest pain. I take ibuprofen every day for longstanding aches and have been using other NSAID pain relievers regularly as well. I have not had this much bleeding before and would appreciate being checked soon.
Model_Diagnosis: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease

Symptoms: rectal bleeding with darker-than-usual stools; fatigue; racing heart when walking; mild abdominal cramping; lightheadedness on standing
Case_History_Text: EMS reports a 34-year-old man, a welder, who was found at home after calling for assistance and arrived alone. He says that over the last three hours he has noticed bleeding with bowel movements and stools darker than usual, along with increasing fatigue. He describes a racing heartbeat when walking, mild intermittent abdominal cramping, and lightheadedness on standing, without fainting. He has strained with bowel movements for years and takes ibuprofen daily for recurring pain. On arrival he is awake, speaking clearly, and has similar, nonconcerning vital signs during transport.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding from NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease

Symptoms: dark stool with a small amount of bright-red blood; mild abdominal cramping; fatigue
Case_History_Text: A 60-year-old woman, who works as a city bus driver, presents to the emergency department with her adult daughter after noticing an unusually dark, sticky bowel movement approximately 45 minutes ago. She reports a small amount of bright-red blood on the toilet paper and in the bowl but is unsure whether it came from the stool or occurred separately. She describes mild, intermittent lower abdominal cramping without severe pain, vomiting, fever, or diarrhea. She has felt more tired than usual today but denies fainting, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath. Her daughter says she appeared worried but has remained alert and able to walk normally. The patient takes an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory pain reliever daily for chronic knee discomfort and reports no recent medication changes. She does not recall a similar episode and has not noticed a definite change in bowel habits before today.
Model_Diagnosis: NSAID-induced bleeding peptic ulcer (upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage)

Symptoms: syncope; lightheadedness; brief confusion afterward; nausea; generalized weakness
Case_History_Text: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her neighbor after an episode of syncope approximately 45 minutes ago. She reports feeling lightheaded while standing in her kitchen after returning from a short walk, followed by a sensation of warmth, mild nausea, and then loss of awareness. Her neighbor witnessed her become unresponsive and lower to the floor without apparent injury. She was unresponsive briefly and became alert within a minute, though she seemed confused and repeatedly asked what had happened. She denies having a clear warning before the event and is unsure whether she experienced palpitations. Since then, she has felt mildly weak and intermittently lightheaded but has had no recurrent loss of consciousness. She denies headache, focal weakness, seizure-like movements, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath. She has diabetes managed as an outpatient and reports no recent medication changes. Her neighbor states that she appeared back to her usual self before arrival.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; slow return of color; dehydration
Case_History_Text: I’m 25 and work as a nurse. Since yesterday I’ve felt unusually lightheaded and probably haven’t been drinking enough, especially with my diabetes and a busy shift. This morning I became nauseated while standing in my kitchen and then fainted, according to my neighbor. I don’t remember much warning before it happened. When I came around, I was on the floor, and my neighbor said I looked very pale and that my color returned slowly. I felt weak and unsteady afterward, with brief waves of near-fainting when I tried to sit up. EMS was called, and they brought me to the emergency department. My neighbor came with me. I have not had a similar episode this severe before, though I’ve occasionally felt lightheaded when dehydrated.
Model_Diagnosis: Syncope due to dehydration-related orthostatic hypotension

Symptoms: syncope/near-syncope; lightheadedness; palpitations; diaphoresis; slow return of color
Case_History_Text: 71-year-old woman, rideshare driver, arrives to ED with spouse for fainting and intermittent near-fainting since last night. Reports lightheadedness while seated in her vehicle, followed by sweating, palpitations, and loss of awareness on one episode. Spouse states her face remained pale and color returned slowly; no clear warning was noted. She feels washed out today and becomes dizzy when standing. Taking a beta blocker. Spouse recalls a heart murmur mentioned years ago but never evaluated. Limited fluids during a busy workday yesterday. Denies recent injury. Triage note: placed in monitored bed for evaluation.
Model_Diagnosis: Severe aortic stenosis causing cardiogenic syncope

Symptoms: intermittent lightheadedness; fainting or near-fainting; nausea; slow return of normal color; possible dehydration
Case_History_Text: I am his daughter, and I came to the emergency department with my father after his neighbor rode with him in the ambulance. He is 65 and works as a construction foreman. Since yesterday evening, he has had episodes of feeling lightheaded and needing to sit down. This morning, while standing in the kitchen, he briefly slumped and seemed to lose awareness. His neighbor helped him into a chair and called EMS. He looked unusually pale, and his color returned slowly. He felt nauseated afterward but has not vomited. My father says he has been drinking very little water during several busy days at work and may be dehydrated. He has had another spell of near-fainting while waiting here.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; palpitations; sudden weakness
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 23-year-old woman and a construction foreman. My adult daughter brought me to the emergency department because I have felt lightheaded and unusually weak for most of today. I briefly lost consciousness once while standing at work and nearly fainted again later, but I do not remember a clear warning before either episode. I felt nauseated afterward and have noticed my heart seeming to pound or pause at times. I did not report chest discomfort or trouble breathing. I have diabetes and take a prescribed beta blocker; I took my usual medications this morning. I have not had a similar episode recently. My daughter says I looked pale and was slow to respond for a short time after the first event.
Model_Diagnosis: Symptomatic bradyarrhythmia due to beta-blocker effect

Symptoms: syncope or near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; palpitations; brief confusion afterward; slow return of normal color
Case_History_Text: EMS brought a 28-year-old man from home to the emergency department with his spouse after a witnessed fainting episode about two hours ago. He works as a postal worker and reported feeling lightheaded and nauseated after a busy, warm shift with limited fluid intake. He noticed intermittent palpitations, then slumped briefly while standing; his spouse said his color returned slowly. He was confused for approximately one minute afterward but became conversational before our arrival. He reports a recent increase in his blood pressure medicine, which includes a beta blocker. No injury was reported.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; delayed return of normal color; possible dehydration
Case_History_Text: A 73-year-old retired accountant was brought to the emergency department by her spouse after an episode of passing out approximately six hours earlier. She reports that she had been feeling somewhat dehydrated after spending the morning running errands and drinking less than usual. While standing in the kitchen, she developed lightheadedness, nausea, and a sensation that she might faint.
