Her spouse observed her become pale and briefly lose consciousness, with no reported injury. She regained awareness within a short time but remained washed out and slow to regain her usual color. Since then, she has had intermittent lightheadedness and mild nausea, particularly when upright, though she has not had recurrent loss of consciousness. She denies recent fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or significant bleeding. Her spouse says she has seemed more tired than usual today. She is currently conversant and able to provide a clear history, while her spouse adds details about the event.

Symptoms: fainting episode; near-syncope; lightheadedness; sweating; brief confusion afterward; slow return of normal color
Case_History_Text: I am a 79-year-old man who works as an office administrator. About three hours ago, while standing in the kitchen with my wife, I became very lightheaded and started sweating. My vision narrowed, and I either fainted briefly or came very close to it; my wife says I slumped against the counter and looked unusually pale. It took several minutes for my color to return, and I was confused for about a minute afterward. I have continued to feel weak and unsteady since then, so my wife called EMS and came with me to the emergency department. I have diabetes and think I may be dehydrated because I have been drinking very little today. I do not recall any injury.

Symptoms: syncope/near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; diaphoresis; transient pallor; fatigue
Case_History_Text: 35-year-old woman, retail manager, brought to ED by coworker after a brief collapse or near-collapse at work approx 45 min ago. Coworker reports she became pale and was slow to regain normal color; duration of unresponsiveness unclear. Pt recalls feeling lightheaded, nauseated, and sweaty beforehand but describes no clear warning. Now awake and answering appropriately, with persistent mild lightheadedness. Reports poor oral intake today and possible dehydration. Blood pressure medication was increased recently. PMH includes diabetes. Denies known injury. No family member present; coworker provides collateral history.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; sudden collapse; fatigue
Case_History_Text: I am his older sister, providing the history after meeting him in the emergency department. He is a 34-year-old college student who had been alone at his apartment when EMS was called. Over the past day, he mentioned feeling unusually lightheaded and tired, with intermittent nausea. This afternoon, while standing in the kitchen, he said he felt faint and then briefly lost consciousness. He was awake again within moments but remained pale, unsteady, and worried that he might pass out again. He cannot describe a clear warning before the episode, although he recalls feeling vaguely sick beforehand. He has not had a similar event that I know of. Several years ago, a clinician mentioned hearing a murmur during a routine visit, but he never had it evaluated.

Symptoms: syncope or near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; slow return of color; brief confusion afterward
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 78-year-old retired nurse who came to the emergency department with my neighbor. Since last night, I have had repeated spells of lightheadedness and feeling as though I might pass out. This morning, while standing in the kitchen, I briefly lost awareness and slid into a chair. My neighbor said my face looked pale and that it took a little while for my color to return. I felt nauseated beforehand and was confused for about a minute afterward, but I could answer questions normally later. I have diabetes and have been told I have a heart murmur, though it has never been evaluated. I do not recall any injury.

Symptoms: Syncope or near-syncope; lightheadedness; intermittent nausea; sweating before episodes; slow return of color
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 75-year-old man, retired mechanic, brought in by his daughter after we were called to their home. He reports episodes of lightheadedness with near-fainting on and off since yesterday evening, including one brief loss of awareness while seated at the kitchen table. He describes no consistent warning, though nausea and sweating occurred before at least one event. His daughter noticed that his color returned slowly afterward. He has diabetes, takes a beta blocker, and was told he had anemia last year. He remained conversational during transport, with his daughter at the bedside.

Symptoms: near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; sweating; generalized weakness
Case_History_Text: A 50-year-old woman who works as an accountant presents to the emergency department with her adult daughter after feeling faint repeatedly over most of today. She reports intermittent lightheadedness and several episodes in which her vision dimmed and she had to sit or lie down, but she did not clearly lose consciousness or sustain an injury. Before the first episode, she felt nauseated, warm, and sweaty. Similar sensations recurred later while she was standing at home and briefly while walking through a grocery store. She denies headache, focal weakness, difficulty speaking, or recent trauma. She has not noticed a clear pattern of rapid or irregular heartbeat. Her daughter says the patient appeared pale and quiet during one episode but remained responsive. She has had reduced food and fluid intake since yesterday because of a busy work deadline and believes she may be dehydrated. She reports no recent medication changes and came in for evaluation because the episodes continued despite resting and drinking some water.

Symptoms: fainting episode; lightheadedness; palpitations; brief confusion afterward; slow return of normal color; possible dehydration
Case_History_Text: I’m 32 and work as an office administrator. About two hours ago, while standing in the kitchen after getting home, I suddenly felt lightheaded and noticed my heart fluttering. I remember becoming sweaty and telling my spouse that I might pass out, then I lost awareness briefly. My spouse says I looked very pale and was slow to regain my usual color. I was confused for about a minute afterward, but I knew where I was soon after that. I still feel washed out and intermittently lightheaded, though I have not fainted again. EMS was called, and my spouse came with me to the emergency department. I may not have drunk enough water today, and I take a beta blocker prescribed for occasional episodes of a racing heartbeat.
Model_Diagnosis: Cardiac syncope due to paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia

Symptoms: syncope/near-syncope; lightheadedness; palpitations; nausea; diaphoresis; transient loss of awareness
Case_History_Text: 19-year-old woman, college student, presents to ED with her adult daughter after an episode of syncope about 6 hrs ago. She reports intermittent lightheadedness and palpitations today, then became sweaty and nauseated before briefly losing awareness while standing. She denies a clear warning and is unsure how long she was unresponsive. No reported injury. PMH includes diabetes, an undiagnosed heart murmur, and hypertension; BP medication was increased recently. Still feels intermittently lightheaded but is speaking clearly and ambulatory at triage. No prior evaluation of the murmur documented.
Model_Diagnosis: Cardiogenic syncope due to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; sweating; sudden weakness
Case_History_Text: I’m his sister, and I came with our neighbor after EMS was called to his apartment. He is 31 and works as a retail manager. Over the past three hours, he has had repeated spells of feeling lightheaded and suddenly weak. During one episode, he became sweaty and briefly slumped to the floor; our neighbor said he was unresponsive for a short time, though he woke before EMS arrived. He has also felt as if he might pass out while sitting and standing, without a clear warning beforehand. He denies chest discomfort, trouble breathing, headache, or recent illness. His blood pressure medicine was increased recently, but I do not know the exact dose or timing. He is now awake but still feels unsteady.

Symptoms: syncope or near-syncope; lightheadedness; sweating before episode; slow return of normal color; no clear warning
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 25-year-old woman and work as a welder. About 45 minutes ago, while standing at work, I suddenly became very lightheaded and sweaty and then either fainted briefly or came close to fainting. My adult daughter brought me to the emergency department, and I still feel unsettled when I sit up. She says I looked unusually pale and that my color returned slowly. I do not recall a clear warning before it happened, though I remember feeling overheated and weak. I have not had a similar episode recently. I take a beta blocker and a blood pressure medication; the blood pressure dose was increased recently. I would appreciate an evaluation.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; sweating; nausea; slow return of normal color
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 69-year-old man brought from home to the emergency department with his spouse after an episode of passing out today. His wife reports he had seemed lightheaded and sweaty beforehand but gave no clear warning before becoming unresponsive briefly while standing. His color returned slowly, and he felt nauseated afterward. He describes intermittent lightheadedness over the past day with reduced fluid intake and a sense of dehydration. He has diabetes and works as a high school coach. His spouse also reports that a heart murmur was noted years ago but was never evaluated.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; diaphoresis; slow return of color
Case_History_Text: An 85-year-old woman, a retired nurse, presents to the emergency department with her neighbor for recurrent lightheadedness and an episode of syncope beginning last night. She reports feeling generally well until she became warm, sweaty, and faint while standing in her kitchen after dinner. She sat down but briefly lost consciousness, with her neighbor stating that she was unresponsive for less than a minute. Her color returned slowly afterward, and she felt tired and mildly unsteady for several minutes. Since then, she has had intermittent waves of lightheadedness and two episodes in which she felt she might pass out, particularly while standing, without another definite loss of consciousness. She denies injury, seizure-like movements, tongue biting, or loss of bladder control. She reports no focal weakness, new difficulty speaking, or persistent confusion. Her medical history includes hypertension, and she takes a beta blocker along with her usual medications. Her neighbor says she has seemed quieter than usual today.

Symptoms: Intermittent lightheadedness since yesterday evening; two near-fainting episodes; one brief loss of awareness; sweating beforehand; confusion for about a minute afterward; feeling dehydrated
Case_History_Text: I’m 20 and work at a daycare. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had episodes where I suddenly feel lightheaded and have to sit or hold onto something. I don’t always get much warning, although I noticed sweating just before one episode. This morning, I was standing in my kitchen and apparently lost awareness briefly; my neighbor found me and said I looked pale. When I came around, I was confused for about a minute, then felt mostly normal except for weakness and thirst. I’ve been drinking less than usual and may be dehydrated. The symptoms have come and gone since last night. My neighbor stayed with me and called EMS, who brought me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; palpitations; nausea; brief post-event confusion
Case_History_Text: 85-y/o woman, retired accountant, brought to ED by neighbor after fainting briefly at home this afternoon. Reports lightheadedness and nausea for most of today, with intermittent awareness of a racing or pounding heartbeat. She had little fluid intake and feels dehydrated; antihypertensive medication was increased recently. Neighbor states pt became pale, slumped in a chair, and was unresponsive briefly, then remained confused for about 1 min. Color returned slowly. No reported injury. Currently awake and answering questions, but still feels weak and intermittently lightheaded.

Symptoms: syncope; lightheadedness; brief confusion afterward; slow return of normal color
Case_History_Text: I am his sister, and our neighbor brought my 33-year-old brother to the emergency department after EMS was called. About two hours ago, while standing in the kitchen after coming home from his nursing shift, he said he felt lightheaded and needed to sit down. Before he could, he became limp and unresponsive for less than a minute. His face looked gray, and it took several minutes for his usual color to return. He was confused for about a minute afterward but then answered questions appropriately. He has continued to feel intermittently lightheaded, without describing pain or shortness of breath. He has never had a similar episode that I know of. A clinician once mentioned hearing a murmur during a school physical, but he never had it evaluated.

Symptoms: syncope; near-syncope; lightheadedness; nausea; palpitations; sweating; weakness
Case_History_Text: Hello, I am a 78-year-old woman and a rideshare driver. About six hours ago, while waiting between passengers, I suddenly felt lightheaded, sweaty, and nauseated, with a fluttering sensation in my chest. I sat down but briefly lost awareness, according to my coworker, who was nearby. Since then I have had several spells of feeling faint and weak, especially when standing, though I have not fallen or injured myself. I have been drinking very little today because of a busy schedule and warm weather. I take a beta blocker regularly and took my usual dose this morning. My coworker brought me to the emergency department because the episodes keep recurring and I still feel unsteady.
Model_Diagnosis: Symptomatic bradycardia due to beta-blocker effect

Symptoms: Syncope or near-syncope; lightheadedness; diaphoresis; palpitations; nausea
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: This is a 59-year-old man, a postal worker, brought in with his spouse after we were called to their home. Over the past three hours, he has had several episodes of marked lightheadedness and one brief collapse or near-collapse while standing, with no clear warning, though his spouse noticed sweating beforehand. He reports intermittent palpitations and nausea but no reported injury. He has been drinking less than usual while working and may be dehydrated. History includes diabetes and use of a beta blocker. He was alert when we arrived and remained so during transport.

Symptoms: syncope; lightheadedness; transient unresponsiveness; slow return of normal color; generalized weakness
Case_History_Text: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her adult daughter after an episode at work approximately 45 minutes ago. She is a warehouse supervisor and had been walking between the loading area and office when she suddenly felt lightheaded and became briefly unresponsive, collapsing into a seated coworker’s arms. She reports no definite warning, although she recalls a vague sensation of warmth and dimming vision immediately beforehand. There was no witnessed shaking, tongue injury, or loss of bladder control. Her daughter says the patient opened her eyes within seconds but remained pale and slow to regain her usual color and alertness. She now feels weak and mildly lightheaded but denies chest discomfort, shortness of breath, headache, focal weakness, or recent illness. She has diabetes managed outside the hospital and reports no prior similar event. Her daughter states that the patient had eaten earlier in the day and had been working her usual shift.

Symptoms: altered mental status; headache; unsteady gait; recent fall; urinary frequency
Case_History_Text: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by a neighbor for approximately 45 minutes of unusual behavior and confusion. The neighbor reports that she was found standing in the hallway of her apartment, repeatedly asking what day it was and appearing unsure where her bathroom was. She had complained of a dull headache earlier in the evening and has seemed unsteady while walking. The patient acknowledges feeling “off” but cannot provide a consistent account of the events. She reportedly stumbled and fell against a padded chair yesterday, without a witnessed loss of consciousness; she did not seek care at that time. Over the past day, the neighbor also noticed more frequent trips to the bathroom and mild irritability. At baseline, she lives independently, works part-time as a graphic designer, and is usually organized and conversational. Her history includes a prior clot for which she takes a daily blood thinner. No seizure-like activity, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath has been observed.

Symptoms: confusion; sleepiness; poor oral intake; unsteady gait; generalized weakness; recent fall
Case_History_Text: I am 86 years old and retired from teaching. My son brought me to the emergency department after EMS was called because I have seemed confused since yesterday. I remember feeling unusually sleepy and weak, but I am not sure what happened this morning. I have barely eaten or drank anything since yesterday and have been unsteady even with my walker. My son says I asked the same questions repeatedly and tried to leave the house without my shoes. I live alone and usually manage with some mild memory trouble. I may have fallen in my hallway two nights ago, although I do not recall striking my head or losing consciousness. I deny knowing of any other recent injury.

Symptoms: Altered mental status since last night; headache; unsteady gait; increased sleepiness; poor oral intake
Case_History_Text: 69-year-old woman brought to ED alone for confusion noted since last night. Patient is a retail manager who lives alone and uses a walker. Reports feeling sleepy, with poor appetite and a mild headache. She appears unsure of the date and gives limited history; states she has been unsteady when walking. Ground-level fall at home last week, with no clear details available. History includes recurrent urinary infections. No family or caregiver present at triage. Respirations even; speaking in short but coherent responses.

Symptoms: altered mental status; intermittent sleepiness; unsteady gait; increased confusion; mild memory problems; possible fall
Case_History_Text: I brought my 69-year-old husband to the emergency department after calling EMS because he has seemed unlike himself on and off since yesterday evening. He works at a neighborhood daycare and is usually active, though he has had mild memory problems for the past year. Last night he became unusually sleepy and asked the same questions several times. This morning he was unsteady while walking and needed to hold onto the furniture. He may have stumbled in the hallway and lowered himself to the floor, but I did not see a clear injury. Since then, he has alternated between answering appropriately and staring quietly, and he seemed confused about where he was. He has not complained clearly of pain, but he has been difficult to keep awake.

Symptoms: New confusion, headache, unsteady gait, low-grade fever, sleepiness, urinary urgency, and a recent fall with uncertain head impact.
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m writing for my 89-year-old neighbor, a retired postal worker. About two hours ago, he became unusually confused and sleepy, complained of a dull headache, and needed help walking because he was unsteady. He has felt warm and has been going to the bathroom more urgently than usual. Earlier today, he stumbled while turning near his porch steps and cannot clearly remember whether he struck his head. His usual mild memory trouble is present, but this change is much more noticeable. He takes a blood thinner after a prior clot and has diabetes and high blood pressure. I called EMS and came with him to the emergency department.

Symptoms: Confusion, disorientation, urinary frequency, headache, and recent fall
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: 88-year-old woman, a retired office administrator, brought alone to the emergency department after a neighbor noticed increasing confusion over roughly six hours. She repeatedly asked the same questions and was unsure of the date. She reports urinary frequency since yesterday and a moderate headache that began this afternoon. She also recalls losing her balance and falling at home two days ago but is uncertain whether she struck her head. She takes a blood thinner following a prior clot. No family or medication list accompanied her, and her usual mental status could not be confirmed.

Symptoms: Confusion, unusual sleepiness, unsteady gait, and increased urinary frequency over the last three hours; recent fall with uncertain head impact.
Case_History_Text: A 78-year-old retired postal worker was brought to the emergency department by EMS with his adult son for three hours of increasing confusion and unusual sleepiness. His son reports that the patient was conversing normally earlier today but later began answering questions slowly, repeating himself, and appearing unsure of where he was. When he stood, he was markedly unsteady and needed assistance to avoid falling. He has also been urinating more frequently since yesterday, although he has not clearly reported pain with urination. Two days ago, he lost his balance while stepping off a curb and fell onto his side. He denied striking his head at the time, but the event was unwitnessed, and his recall is now limited. There has been no reported fainting, seizure-like activity, vomiting, or new one-sided weakness. His history includes diabetes and high blood pressure, and he takes a blood thinner following a prior clot.

Symptoms: Confusion, unusual sleepiness, poor oral intake, low-grade fever, headache, urinary urgency, and recent fall
Case_History_Text: I’m 69 and work as a graphic designer. My coworker brought me to the emergency department because for the past 45 minutes I’ve seemed confused and unusually sleepy. I’m having trouble recalling parts of this morning and finding the right words, although I already have mild memory problems. I have a dull headache and haven’t eaten or drunk much today. I’ve also felt mildly feverish and have needed to urinate more urgently than usual, without much coming out. Yesterday I stumbled over a rug and sat down hard on the floor; I don’t remember striking my head, but I’m not completely sure. I take a blood thinner after a prior clot and have diabetes and high blood pressure.

Symptoms: Confusion, low-grade fever, unsteady gait, urinary urgency, mild headache, fatigue
Case_History_Text: 72M retired mechanic brought to ED alone by EMS after a neighbor found him confused and walking unsteadily. Symptoms reportedly began during the past day. Pt gives inconsistent answers, feels fatigued, and reports urinary urgency without flank pain. Also notes a mild, diffuse headache. Neighbor relayed that pt had a ground-level fall last week; pt recalls no loss of consciousness and is unsure whether he struck his head. Temp 100.2 F, HR 92, BP 146/84, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA.

Symptoms: Confusion, unusual sleepiness, poor oral intake, and unsteady walking since last night.
Case_History_Text: I brought my 76-year-old mother to the emergency department because she has not seemed like herself since last night. She is normally independent and still works as a rideshare driver, but today she was confused about the time, answered questions slowly, and kept drifting off while sitting. She has eaten and drunk very little and needed my help walking because she was unusually unsteady. Last week, she had a ground-level fall while stepping off a curb. She did not lose consciousness and continued her usual activities afterward, though she mentioned feeling generally sore. She has diabetes and high blood pressure. I have not noticed facial drooping, slurred speech, shaking, vomiting, or another fall.

Symptoms: Intermittent confusion, unusual sleepiness, urinary frequency, unsteady gait, and low-grade fever since yesterday evening.
Case_History_Text: My 75-year-old father, a retired mechanic, was brought to the emergency department by EMS after I found him unusually sleepy and confused. His symptoms have come and gone since yesterday evening. He has been asking the same questions, losing track of conversations, and needing help to walk because he seems unsteady. He has also been going to the bathroom much more often than usual and felt mildly feverish. This morning, he stumbled while getting out of bed and lowered himself awkwardly to the floor; neither of us is certain whether he struck his head. He has had recurrent urinary infections in the past and takes a blood thinner because of a prior clot. This behavior and balance difficulty are not normal for him.
Model_Diagnosis: Urinary tract infection causing acute delirium

Symptoms: Confusion, unusual sleepiness, unsteady gait, urinary urgency, and lower abdominal discomfort
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: 87-year-old woman, retired postal worker, brought to the emergency department with her spouse for confusion and unusual sleepiness lasting most of today. Spouse reports she has needed assistance walking because she is more unsteady than usual and has repeatedly asked where she is. She has also complained of urinary urgency and mild lower abdominal discomfort since yesterday. Three days ago, she lost her balance while getting out of bed and struck the side of her head on a nightstand, without reported loss of consciousness. History includes diabetes and high blood pressure.

Symptoms: Acute confusion, disorientation, unsteady gait, headache, low-grade fever, urinary urgency, and increased urinary frequency
Case_History_Text: A 92-year-old retired welder was brought alone to the emergency department after EMS was called by a neighbor who noticed him wandering outside and speaking incoherently. His confusion began approximately two hours before arrival. He is intermittently oriented to his name but not to place or date, answers some questions appropriately, and repeatedly asks why he is in the hospital. He reports a dull, diffuse headache and feels feverish. He also describes urinary urgency and more frequent voiding since yesterday but cannot provide further details. When attempting to walk, he is unsteady and requires assistance, which he says is unusual for him. He recalls a ground-level fall at home one week ago after tripping over a rug but is uncertain whether he struck his head. He takes a blood-thinning medication following a prior clot. No family or caregiver is present to clarify his usual mental status or recent symptoms.

Symptoms: I feel confused, sleepy, unsteady, and headachy, with little appetite and frequent, uncomfortable urination.
Case_History_Text: I’m 73 and work as a home health aide. My neighbor brought me to the emergency department because for about six hours I haven’t seemed like myself. I keep losing track of what I’m saying, feel unusually sleepy, and have a dull headache. When I stand, I’m wobbly even with my walker. I have barely eaten or drunk anything today. Since yesterday, I’ve also needed to urinate more often, with some lower abdominal discomfort. I live alone. Last week I tripped at home and fell from standing height; I don’t clearly remember whether I struck my head, but I did not seek care then. I take a blood thinner because of a previous clot.

Symptoms: Acute confusion, sleepiness, headache, urinary urgency, burning with urination, recent fall
Case_History_Text: 91M, retired postal worker, BIB EMS with neighbor for confusion and increased sleepiness over last 3 hrs. Neighbor reports pt repeatedly asked the same questions and was difficult to keep awake. Pt c/o dull headache, urinary urgency, and burning with urination since yesterday. Had an unwitnessed ground-level fall at home 2 days ago; unsure whether head was struck. Takes a blood thinner after prior clot. No reported vomiting, fever, focal weakness, facial droop, or slurred speech. On arrival, drowsy but arousable, oriented to name only.

Symptoms: Sudden confusion, unusual sleepiness, low-grade fever, poor oral intake, and unsteady walking
Case_History_Text: My mother is 79 and a retired accountant. I brought her to the emergency department because over the past 45 minutes she has become noticeably confused and much sleepier than usual. She answers simple questions slowly, repeats herself, and briefly seemed unsure where she was. She has eaten and drunk very little since yesterday and felt mildly feverish this morning. Earlier today, she stumbled while walking to the bathroom and lowered herself against the wall; I did not see her strike her head, and she did not lose consciousness. She has diabetes and high blood pressure. In the past, she has had several episodes of urinary frequency and burning, although she has not clearly reported those symptoms today.

Symptoms: Confusion, poor oral intake, low-grade fever, unsteady gait, urinary frequency, and possible recent fall.
Case_History_Text: I am his coworker and came with him after we called EMS. He is a 75-year-old home health aide who has seemed unusually confused over the past day. He has eaten and drunk very little, felt mildly feverish, and has been going to the bathroom more often than usual. His walking is shakier even with his walker. He told me he may have stumbled at home yesterday but cannot clearly recall whether he fell or struck his head. He has mild baseline memory problems, but this is a noticeable change. He lives alone and takes a blood-thinning medicine after a previous clot. Today he had trouble following simple questions and needed help standing safely.
Model_Diagnosis: Urinary tract infection causing acute delirium

Symptoms: Confusion since last night, unsteady gait, low-grade fever, and mild headache after a ground-level fall last week.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff to the emergency department: We brought in an 86-year-old woman who works as a high school coach. Her neighbor found her confused this morning after she had seemed normal yesterday evening. She has been repeating questions, misplacing items, and walking more unsteadily than usual. She reports a mild headache and feeling chilled but denies vomiting or loss of consciousness. The neighbor reports a ground-level fall last week without immediate symptoms. On arrival, she is awake but disoriented to date, with temperature 100.2°F, blood pressure 146/78, pulse 88, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Symptoms: Intermittent confusion, low-grade fever, urinary frequency, poor oral intake, generalized weakness, unsteady gait, and a recent fall.
Case_History_Text: An 82-year-old nonbinary adult who works part-time as a home health aide was brought to the emergency department by EMS with their adult child. Since yesterday evening, they have had intermittent confusion, at times answering questions appropriately and at other times appearing disoriented, forgetful, or unusually drowsy. Their child reports a low-grade fever, increased urinary frequency, poor oral intake, generalized weakness, and an unsteady gait during the same period. Earlier yesterday, the patient had a fall while walking from the bedroom to the bathroom; the event was not witnessed, and the patient cannot clearly recall whether they struck their head or lost consciousness. The child has not observed vomiting, seizure-like activity, one-sided weakness, facial asymmetry, or difficulty speaking. The patient reports no severe headache, neck pain, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or painful urination. Their history is notable for taking a blood thinner after a prior clot.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute delirium due to urinary tract infection

Symptoms: I have been confused, forgetful, unsteady on my feet, and unusually tired most of today. I also have a headache, poor appetite, increased urination, and thirst.
Case_History_Text: I’m 89 and a retired welder. My spouse brought me to the emergency department because I haven’t seemed like myself for most of today. I keep losing track of what I’m saying and had trouble finding my bathroom. I’ve been urinating more often than usual, though I don’t remember any burning. My head aches, and I feel wobbly even with my walker. I barely ate or drank today. I live alone and usually manage despite mild memory problems. Yesterday, I stumbled while turning with my walker and ended up sitting on the floor; I’m not sure whether I bumped my head. I have diabetes and high blood pressure.

Symptoms: Acute confusion, sleepiness, repetitive questioning, urinary urgency, and unsteady gait.
Case_History_Text: Triage: 90M retired teacher brought to ED by EMS with former coworker. Coworker reports abrupt change from baseline over ~2 hrs: increasingly sleepy, slow to answer, intermittently disoriented, and repeating questions. Gait newly unsteady; required assistance walking. Pt reports urinary urgency since yesterday but gives inconsistent history and denies focal pain. Ground-level fall last week while stepping off a curb; pt unsure whether head was struck, with no reported loss of consciousness. No vomiting, fever, unilateral weakness, facial droop, or witnessed seizure. Baseline reportedly alert, independent, and conversational.

Symptoms: Confusion, unusual sleepiness, urinary frequency, and unsteady gait for about six hours; possible minor fall earlier in the day.
Case_History_Text: My mother is a 70-year-old retired postal worker. She came into the emergency department alone after I dropped her near the entrance because I had to park. For roughly six hours, she has seemed confused and much sleepier than usual. She has repeatedly asked what day it is and misplaced familiar belongings. She has also been going to the bathroom more often, although she has not mentioned pain. When walking, she drifts to one side and needs to hold furniture for balance. She may have slipped while getting out of bed this morning, but she cannot clearly recall whether she struck anything. She takes a blood thinner after a prior clot and has had recurrent urinary infections. Before today, she managed her own medications and daily activities.

Symptoms: New confusion, repetitive questions, low-grade fever, unsteady gait, poor oral intake, headache, frequent urination, discomfort while passing urine, and a recent fall with possible head impact.
Case_History_Text: Emergency team, my 89-year-old father, a retired postal worker, became noticeably confused over the last three hours. He has been repeating questions, misplacing familiar items, and needing help to walk because he seems unusually unsteady. He reports a steady headache and has felt mildly feverish. He has eaten and drunk very little today. He has also gone to the bathroom several times and appeared uncomfortable while passing urine. Yesterday, he slipped while getting out of a chair and may have bumped the side of his head, although no one saw a loss of consciousness. His history includes diabetes, high blood pressure, mild memory problems, and use of a blood thinner after a prior clot. I arrived with him after calling EMS.

Symptoms: Sudden confusion, unusual sleepiness, unsteady gait, urinary urgency, and mild headache after a recent fall.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 92-year-old woman who works as an accountant, accompanied by her spouse. Over the past 45 minutes, she became confused, unusually sleepy, and unsteady while using her walker. Her spouse reports urinary urgency since yesterday without visible blood or flank discomfort. She lives alone and normally manages her daily activities independently. Two days ago, she slipped beside her bed and may have struck the side of her head, but she did not seek care. She now reports a mild headache and cannot clearly recall the fall. No vomiting or witnessed seizure activity.

Symptoms: Acute confusion, disorientation, headache, reduced appetite, low fluid intake, generalized weakness, unsteady walking, and uncertain recent fall history.
Case_History_Text: An 81-year-old woman who previously worked as a retail manager presents alone to the emergency department after arriving by taxi. Over the past 45 minutes, staff have observed fluctuating confusion: she repeatedly asks why she is present, misplaces personal items, and gives inconsistent answers about the date. She reports a dull, diffuse headache but cannot clearly state when it began or whether it has worsened. She describes eating and drinking very little since yesterday because she has not felt hungry. She feels generally weak and more unsteady than usual. The patient lives alone and normally walks with a walker. When asked about recent injury, she first denies falling, then recalls possibly slipping beside her bed several days ago but is unsure whether she struck her head or lost awareness. She denies current chest discomfort, shortness of breath, vomiting, focal weakness, or vision loss. No family member or caregiver is available to clarify her recent baseline or events at home.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, burning with urination, urinary frequency, backache, and rapid breathing noticed by family.
Case_History_Text: A 66-year-old man who works as a pharmacist was brought to the emergency department by EMS after his spouse became concerned about fever, increasing fatigue, and faster breathing over the past day. He reports burning with urination and needing to void more often than usual, with several small-volume episodes since yesterday morning. He also describes a dull, constant ache across his lower back without radiation. His spouse states that he has seemed less energetic, has spent much of the day resting, and was breathing more quickly while seated, prompting the EMS call. He denies chest pain, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, visible blood in the urine, fainting, or new confusion. He has had reduced appetite but has been able to drink fluids. His history is notable for diabetes managed with daily medication. At arrival, he is awake, conversant, and able to provide a coherent history, though he appears tired and mildly uncomfortable.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, backache, burning with urination, muscle aches, and faster breathing noticed by family since last night.
Case_History_Text: I’m 25 and work as a mechanic. Since last night, I’ve felt feverish, drained, and achy all over. My lower back has been hurting, and it burns when I urinate. I’ve also been going more often, though only small amounts come out. My adult stepdaughter brought me to the emergency department because she noticed I was breathing faster than usual while resting. I have diabetes and was recently in the hospital for another problem. During that stay, and occasionally afterward, I had a catheter in place. I haven’t fainted, but I feel weak and generally unwell. I haven’t noticed vomiting, chest pain, or a new rash.

Symptoms: Intermittent fever, malaise, burning with urination, urinary frequency, and dull lower backache since yesterday evening.
Case_History_Text: 46M accountant brought to ED by EMS after adult child called for intermittent fever, chills, fatigue, burning with urination, increased frequency, and dull bilateral lower backache since yesterday evening. Reports reduced appetite and mild nausea without vomiting. Denies chest pain, SOB, cough, abdominal pain, blood in urine, or fainting. Hx diabetes; states home glucose readings have been somewhat higher than usual. Alert, answers questions appropriately, appears tired. T 38.2 C, BP 126/74, HR 99, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, nausea, muscle aches, burning with urination, urinary frequency, and faster breathing noticed by family.
Case_History_Text: I’m her neighbor and brought her to the emergency department because she has seemed increasingly unwell for most of today. She is 28 and works at a daycare. This morning she complained of feeling feverish, exhausted, and achy all over. By afternoon, she was nauseated and had little interest in food or fluids. She also mentioned burning when urinating and needing to go more often than usual, though only small amounts came out. When I checked on her this evening, she was breathing faster than normal while sitting still, and her family had noticed the same thing. She has diabetes and had kidney stones several years ago. She has not described any recent injury or other new symptoms.

Symptoms: Feverishness, malaise, burning with urination, backache, muscle aches, and noticeably fast breathing.
Case_History_Text: I’m a 51-year-old security guard. About two hours ago, I began feeling feverish and generally unwell, with muscle aches and a steady ache across my lower back. Urinating has caused a strong burning sensation, and I feel as though I need to go more often than usual. My family noticed that I was breathing faster, although I did not initially realize it. EMS was called because the symptoms came on quickly, and my neighbor accompanied me to the emergency department. I have had several previous episodes of burning and frequent urination. Years ago, I passed painful hard deposits while urinating, and at different times I have needed a catheter left in place. I have not noticed fainting or severe chest discomfort.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, confusion, backache, urinary frequency, and burning with urination for roughly six hours.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 60-year-old unemployed woman from home, accompanied by her spouse, for about six hours of fever, worsening fatigue, urinary frequency, burning with urination, and a dull lower backache. Her spouse reports she became intermittently confused this evening, asking repeated questions and losing track of the time. She has had recurrent bladder infections with similar urinary discomfort, though the confusion is new. On arrival to the emergency department, temperature was 38.2°C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, nausea, painful urination, urinary urgency, rapid breathing, and confusion developing over three hours.
Case_History_Text: A 26-year-old man who works as a home health aide was brought to the emergency department by EMS with his spouse after three hours of fever, worsening malaise, and nausea. His spouse called EMS because he began breathing faster than usual and seemed confused, repeatedly asking why they were leaving home and giving inconsistent answers about the time. Earlier in the evening, he reported burning discomfort with urination and an urgent need to void several times, producing only small amounts. He denies vomiting, diarrhea, cough, chest discomfort, flank pain, or a recent injury. He has diabetes and was discharged from a hospital five days ago after a brief admission for dehydration. His spouse states that he had appeared well earlier today and had been eating and drinking normally until the symptoms began. On arrival, his temperature is 38.4°C, heart rate 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Model_Diagnosis: Sepsis due to complicated urinary tract infection

Symptoms: Feverishness, malaise, rapid breathing, burning with urination, muscle aches, and nausea
Case_History_Text: I’m 83 and still work part-time as an accountant. About 45 minutes ago, I suddenly began feeling much more feverish and unwell, with aching muscles and nausea. I’ve had burning when I pass urine since earlier today, and I feel like I need to go more often, although only a small amount comes out. My family noticed that I was breathing faster than usual before I left, but I came to the emergency department alone. I have diabetes and have had recurrent bladder infections in the past. At times I need an indwelling catheter, though I do not currently have one. I feel weak and washed out, but I have not fainted or vomited.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, myalgias, dysuria, urinary frequency, chills, reduced appetite
Case_History_Text: 24M postal worker brought to ED after EMS was called; arrives alone. Reports feeling feverish and generally unwell since yesterday, with diffuse muscle aches, intermittent chills, fatigue, reduced appetite, burning with urination, and increased urinary frequency. Denies vomiting, diarrhea, cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, flank pain, or visible blood in urine. States he had kidney stones several years ago but says this feels different. Alert and ambulatory at triage. T 38.2 C, HR 104, BP 124/76, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, nausea, confusion, backache, urinary urgency, and burning with urination since last night.
Case_History_Text: My 69-year-old aunt, who works as a postal worker, was brought to the emergency department by her neighbor. Since last night, she has felt feverish, unusually tired, and generally unwell. She has complained of nausea without vomiting, an aching pain across her lower back, frequent urges to urinate, and burning when she does. This morning, her neighbor noticed that she seemed confused, repeated questions, and had trouble recalling why they were leaving the house. She has diabetes and occasionally uses an indwelling catheter when she has difficulty emptying her bladder. She was able to walk in with assistance but appeared weak and less alert than usual.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, intermittent confusion, rapid breathing, backache, and burning with urination since yesterday evening.
Case_History_Text: I’m a 30-year-old high school coach. My spouse came with me to the emergency department after calling EMS because I seemed confused at times and was breathing faster than usual. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had symptoms that come and go, including fever, feeling weak and generally unwell, an aching pain across my lower back, and burning when I urinate. My spouse says I have occasionally answered questions slowly or seemed unsure about what was happening, although at other times I have felt clearheaded. I have diabetes, have needed an indwelling catheter at times, and have had recurrent bladder infections. I have not noticed any recent injury that would explain the backache.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, muscle aches, backache, urinary frequency, and burning with urination for most of today.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 73-year-old woman from home, accompanied by her adult daughter. She is a retired nurse and reports feeling feverish, unusually tired, and generally unwell since this morning, with diffuse muscle aches and a dull lower backache. She also describes increased urinary frequency and burning with urination. Her daughter says she has been less active today but remains alert and conversational. She intermittently requires an indwelling catheter, though not continuously. En route, temperature was 38.2°C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 132/74, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, burning with urination, confusion, and diffuse muscle aches.
Case_History_Text: A 51-year-old man who works as a graphic designer was brought to the emergency department by EMS with his adult daughter. She called EMS after noticing that, over approximately two hours, he became unusually tired, mildly confused, and less engaged in conversation. He reports feeling feverish with diffuse muscle aches and burning during urination. He has difficulty recalling exactly when the urinary discomfort began but believes it was earlier today. His daughter states he was functioning normally this morning and had completed some work from home before developing chills and lying down. He denies chest discomfort, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, flank pain, or a recent fall. His medical history includes diabetes, and he intermittently uses an indwelling urinary catheter because of chronic difficulty emptying his bladder. On arrival, he appears fatigued and answers most questions appropriately, though he occasionally needs questions repeated. Temperature is 38.2°C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 128/74, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Model_Diagnosis: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection with sepsis-associated encephalopathy

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, muscle aches, nausea, burning with urination, and faster breathing noticed by family.
Case_History_Text: I’m 57 and work on a farm. My daughter brought me to the emergency department because I’ve felt increasingly unwell for about six hours. I started with feverish chills, tiredness, and aching muscles, then developed nausea without vomiting. It burns when I urinate, and I’ve been going more often than usual, though only small amounts come out. My daughter says I have been breathing faster than normal, especially while walking from the car, but I do not feel short of breath while sitting. I have diabetes and had kidney stones several years ago. I felt well earlier today and was able to do my usual farm chores before these symptoms began.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, confusion, urinary frequency, burning with urination, rapid breathing.
Case_History_Text: 85M retired mechanic brought to ED by EMS with adult son. Family called EMS for 3 hrs of increasing confusion, fatigue, and fast breathing. Son reports pt felt feverish and weak, with several urgent trips to urinate and burning during urination. No reported fall, chest discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or flank pain. Hx diabetes. At triage, pt awake but disoriented to date and gives brief answers. T 38.1 C, HR 102, RR 24, BP 132/74, SpO2 95% on room air.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, burning with urination, muscle aches, and confusion
Case_History_Text: I’m her cousin and neighbor, and I brought her to the emergency department because she has become noticeably worse over the past 45 minutes. She is 59 and currently unemployed. She felt feverish and generally unwell earlier today, with aching muscles and burning whenever she urinated. During the last 45 minutes, she became unusually confused, repeated questions, and seemed unsure why we were leaving home. She has been awake and able to answer me, but her responses are slower than usual. She has diabetes and was discharged after a recent hospital stay. I have not noticed vomiting, diarrhea, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, fainting, or a new rash.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, burning and frequent urination, backache, nausea, confusion, and fast breathing noticed by family.
Case_History_Text: Hello emergency team, I’m a 25-year-old farmer. Over the past day I have felt feverish, unusually weak, and generally unwell. I have been urinating more often, with burning and urgency, and I have a dull ache across my lower back. I also feel nauseated and have had little appetite. My family said I was breathing faster than usual and seemed confused, repeating questions and losing track of the conversation, so they called EMS. I arrived at the emergency department alone. I have diabetes and have previously had several similar episodes involving painful, frequent urination. At times I have needed an indwelling urinary catheter, though I do not currently have one.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, burning with urination, urinary frequency, rapid breathing, and confusion since last night.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 56-year-old woman who works as a security guard, accompanied by a coworker. Since last night, she has had fever, generalized malaise, burning with urination, and increased urinary frequency. Family reported that she was breathing faster than usual and seemed confused this morning. She recently had a hospital stay but could not clearly explain the reason. During transport, she remained awake but was intermittently disoriented to time. Door vitals were temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 23, blood pressure 118/72, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

Symptoms: Intermittent fever, malaise, confusion, muscle aches, urinary urgency, burning with urination, increased urinary frequency, reduced appetite, and visibly fast breathing.
Case_History_Text: An 84-year-old nonbinary security guard was brought to the emergency department by EMS, accompanied by their spouse, for symptoms occurring on and off since yesterday evening. Their spouse reports intermittent fever, generalized malaise, diffuse muscle aches, and reduced appetite. During the night, the patient began making repeated trips to the bathroom and complained of urinary urgency, increased frequency, and burning with urination. This morning, they appeared confused, misplaced familiar items, and gave inconsistent answers about the date, which is not typical for them. Family also noticed that they were breathing faster than usual while resting, although the patient denied feeling markedly short of breath. They have had no reported fall, loss of consciousness, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, chest discomfort, flank discomfort, or visible blood in the urine. Their history includes recurrent bladder infections and a recent hospital stay. EMS was called because the confusion and fast breathing persisted despite rest and oral fluids.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, nausea, burning with urination, confusion, and rapid breathing
Case_History_Text: I’m 39 and work as a postal worker. I came to the emergency department with my spouse because I’ve felt feverish, weak, and generally unwell for most of today. I’ve been nauseated but haven’t vomited. It burns when I urinate, and I feel like I need to go more often, though only a small amount comes out. My spouse says I seemed confused earlier and was answering questions oddly. They also noticed that I was breathing faster than usual while resting. I remember feeling foggy, but I’m not sure how long that lasted. I have diabetes, and I sometimes need an indwelling catheter because I have trouble emptying my bladder. I felt mostly normal yesterday.
Model_Diagnosis: Urosepsis due to catheter-associated complicated urinary tract infection

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, confusion, low backache, urinary frequency, burning with urination
Case_History_Text: 74M retired accountant brought to ED by EMS with coworker after coworker noted sudden confusion and marked fatigue beginning about 2 hrs PTA. Pt reports feeling feverish with chills, dull low backache, urinary frequency, and burning with urination. Coworker states pt is normally alert and independent but today repeated questions and appeared unsteady. Hx of recurrent episodes with similar urinary complaints. Denies chest pain, SOB, vomiting, diarrhea, fall, or recent injury. T 38.2 C, HR 96, BP 132/74, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, nausea, lower backache, muscle aches, urinary frequency, and burning with urination.
Case_History_Text: I brought my wife, a 62-year-old office administrator, to the emergency department after she became noticeably unwell over about six hours. She first complained of feeling unusually tired and achy, then developed a fever, nausea, and a dull ache across her lower back. She has also been going to the bathroom more often than usual and says it burns when she urinates. She has not vomited and has remained awake and able to answer questions, though she seems more drained than normal. She has diabetes. At arrival, her temperature was 38.3°C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 128/74, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, nausea, confusion, rapid breathing, and burning with urination for three hours.
Case_History_Text: I’m a 33-year-old restaurant cook, and I’m writing this with help from my spouse because I feel foggy and have trouble answering questions clearly. About three hours ago, I suddenly began feeling feverish, weak, and generally unwell. I became nauseated but have not vomited. My spouse noticed that I was breathing faster than usual and seemed confused, so they called EMS and came with me to the emergency department. I have also had burning when I urinate today. In the past, I’ve had several similar episodes involving bladder discomfort and painful urination. At times, I have needed an indwelling catheter, though I do not normally use one continuously.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, confusion, muscle aches, urinary urgency, frequent urination, and burning with urination.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 64-year-old woman who works as a janitor, accompanied by her adult daughter. Over the past 45 minutes, the daughter noticed increasing confusion and unusual fatigue. The patient reports fever, generalized muscle aches, malaise, urinary urgency, frequent small-volume urination, and burning when passing urine. She denies fainting, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, vomiting, or flank pain. She had kidney stones several years ago but no recent procedures. On arrival to the emergency department, temperature was 38.2°C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 126/74, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Symptoms: Fever, malaise, muscle aches, urinary frequency, burning with urination, and rapid breathing noticed by family
Case_History_Text: A 65-year-old woman who works as a high school coach presents to the emergency department with a neighbor for fever, generalized malaise, and muscle aches. She reports that burning with urination and increased urinary frequency began yesterday, without visible blood or difficulty passing urine. Over the past 45 minutes, she has felt more fatigued and chilled, prompting her neighbor to bring her in. Family members noticed that she seemed to be breathing faster than usual before departure, although the patient denies shortness of breath, chest discomfort, cough, or wheezing. She has had mild nausea but no vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, back pain, fainting, confusion, or new rash. She has diabetes and states that her appetite and fluid intake have been somewhat reduced today. She remains able to answer questions clearly and reports no recent injury, travel, or known exposure to anyone with a contagious illness.

Symptoms: Unilateral right calf pain, swelling, redness, skin tightness, warmth, tenderness, and a mild feverish feeling for one day
Case_History_Text: A 52-year-old man who works as a retail manager arrived in the emergency department by ambulance, accompanied by his adult daughter, for pain and swelling of the right lower leg that developed over the past day. He first noticed tightness of the skin around the calf while at work, followed by increasing soreness and visible swelling. The area has also appeared mildly red and feels warmer than the other leg. Walking and prolonged standing worsen the discomfort, although he remains able to bear weight. He reports feeling mildly feverish but has not measured his temperature. He does not recall a fall, direct blow, muscle strain, or other recent injury. Several days ago, he noticed a small superficial scrape on the affected calf without significant bleeding or drainage. He also returned recently from a several-hour flight. He reports no similar prior episode and no symptoms in the opposite leg.

Symptoms: My left calf has been painful, swollen, warm, and red since last night. It hurts more when I walk, and I feel mildly feverish.
Case_History_Text: I’m 77 and currently unemployed. A coworker from my previous job brought me to the emergency department because my left lower leg became sore and swollen last night. The discomfort is mostly in my calf, and the skin there feels warmer than the other side and looks somewhat red. Walking makes the pain worse, so I’ve been moving more slowly today. I have felt a little feverish, but I have not checked my temperature. I do not remember falling, twisting my leg, or bumping it. I am obese and have peeling, itchy skin between my toes. I also noticed a small scrape on the same calf a few days ago.

Symptoms: Intermittent unilateral right calf pain and swelling since yesterday evening, with skin tightness, mild redness, warmth, and a feverish feeling.
Case_History_Text: 47-y/o man, graphic designer, arrived alone to ED after EMS was called. Reports R lower-leg pain and swelling occurring on and off since yesterday evening. Describes calf as sore and heavy, with tight-feeling skin. Notes mild redness and warmth compared with the other leg and says he has felt slightly feverish, without measured temp. Denies known injury, fall, open wound, drainage, numbness, or weakness. Recently returned from a several-hour flight. Symptoms became more noticeable while walking today, prompting the call to EMS.

Symptoms: Left lower-leg pain, one-sided swelling, redness, warmth, tenderness, pain with walking, and a mild feverish feeling.
Case_History_Text: I’m her sister, and our neighbor drove us to the emergency department because her left lower leg has been hurting and swelling for most of today. She is 61 and works as a construction foreman. This morning she noticed tightness around the calf, and by late afternoon the leg looked more swollen than the other side, with an area of redness and warmth. She says the aching becomes sharper when she walks or puts weight on it. She has felt mildly feverish but has not had shaking chills. She does not remember falling, twisting the leg, being struck at work, or getting a cut. She had abdominal surgery three weeks ago and has been less active during recovery. Her older brother previously had a blood clot in his leg.

Symptoms: Right calf pain, one-sided swelling, redness, skin tightness, pain with walking, mild feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: I am a 36-year-old farmer. About two hours ago, I noticed increasing pain and swelling in my right calf while finishing chores. The area feels tight and looks mildly red, and walking makes the pain worse. I have felt slightly feverish but have not noticed shaking chills. I do not remember twisting the leg, falling, being kicked, or having another injury. There is a small scrape on that calf from several days ago. I recently returned from a long flight and currently use estrogen therapy. The discomfort and swelling seemed to worsen quickly, so EMS was called. I arrived at the emergency department without a family member or other companion.

Symptoms: Unilateral lower-leg pain, swelling, erythema, skin tightness, and a mild feverish feeling for approximately six hours.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We transported a 39-year-old woman who works as a graphic designer and arrived without family or other companions. She reports roughly six hours of gradually increasing pain and swelling in her left lower leg. The skin feels tight, and she has noticed mild redness over the affected area. She also describes feeling slightly feverish but denies shaking chills, fainting, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath. She reports obesity in her medical history. No injury or clear trigger was identified during transport, and her symptoms remained stable en route to the emergency department.

Symptoms: Unilateral lower-leg pain, swelling, erythema, skin tightness, pain with walking, and a mild feverish sensation for three hours.
Case_History_Text: A 47-year-old man who works as a rideshare driver presented to the emergency department accompanied by a coworker after emergency medical services were called for rapidly noticed left lower-leg discomfort. He reports that approximately three hours before arrival, he developed aching pain and swelling below the knee while finishing a driving shift. The affected area has since felt increasingly tight, with mild redness and warmth compared with the opposite leg. Walking and bearing weight worsen the pain, although he remains able to ambulate. He describes feeling mildly feverish but denies shaking chills, fainting, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, or coughing blood. He does not recall a recent fall, direct blow, puncture, or insect bite and has not noticed drainage or an open sore. His history includes diabetes and ongoing estrogen therapy. He reports spending prolonged periods seated while driving and has not previously experienced an episode with this combination of unilateral swelling, redness, and pain.

Symptoms: My left calf hurts and looks swollen and red. The skin feels tight and warm, and I feel mildly feverish.
Case_History_Text: I’m 27 and work as a warehouse supervisor. My coworker brought me to the emergency department because, over the past 45 minutes, I noticed increasing pain and swelling in my left calf. The skin feels tight and warmer than the other side, with some redness around the sore area. I feel a little feverish but otherwise okay. I don’t remember twisting, bumping, or otherwise injuring my leg. I do have peeling, itchy skin between my toes, and there is a small scrape on the same calf from a few days ago. I also returned recently from a flight where I was seated for several hours.

Symptoms: Left lower-leg pain, swelling, redness, skin tightness, and mild feverish feeling for 1 day.
Case_History_Text: 46M rideshare driver presents to ED with neighbor after EMS was called for worsening L lower-leg discomfort over the past day. Reports unilateral calf and ankle swelling with aching pain, diffuse redness, warmth, and tight-feeling skin. Pain worse with walking and prolonged sitting. Felt mildly feverish at home but did not measure temp. Denies known injury, open wound, chest pain, SOB, dizziness, or fainting. Hx recurrent athlete’s foot with recent itching and cracked skin between toes. Alert, ambulatory with limp, speaking full sentences.

Symptoms: Pain and swelling in the left lower leg, skin tightness, redness, warmth, tenderness, and a mild feverish feeling since last night.
Case_History_Text: I brought my mother to the emergency department because her left lower leg became painful and swollen overnight. She is 67 and works as a mechanic, spending much of the day standing, crouching, or working in awkward positions. This morning, she said the skin over her calf felt unusually tight, and I noticed an area of redness and warmth. She has been walking more slowly because putting weight on that leg increases the discomfort. She felt mildly feverish but did not report shaking chills. She does not remember bumping, twisting, cutting, or otherwise injuring the leg. She has diabetes and uses prescribed estrogen therapy. The other leg looks and feels normal, and she had not experienced this type of swelling before.

Symptoms: Right lower-leg pain, swelling, redness, skin tightness, mild feverish feeling, and pain with walking, occurring on and off since yesterday evening.
Case_History_Text: Hello emergency team, I’m a 24-year-old construction foreman here with my neighbor after EMS was called. Since yesterday evening, my right calf and lower leg have been swelling and hurting on and off. The skin feels tight and looks red compared with the other leg. Walking makes the pain worse, and I have felt mildly feverish, though I have not noticed shaking chills. I do not remember falling, twisting the leg, being struck, or having any other injury at work. I recently had surgery and also took a long flight. I am obese. I have not had this exact combination of one-sided swelling, redness, and discomfort before, and it seems more noticeable today.

Symptoms: One-sided lower-leg pain, swelling, redness, warmth, and skin tightness lasting most of the day; no recalled injury.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 25-year-old woman who works as a rideshare driver and is arriving without family or friends. She reports pain and swelling in one lower leg that began earlier today and has gradually become more noticeable. The skin feels tight, with mild redness and warmth over the swollen area. She does not remember twisting, striking, or otherwise injuring the leg. She recently underwent surgery and has spent extended periods seated while working. She remained alert and comfortable at rest during transport to the emergency department.

Symptoms: Left lower-leg pain, swelling, redness, skin tightness, and pain with walking for about two hours; no remembered injury.
Case_History_Text: A 55-year-old unemployed man presented to the emergency department with a neighbor after emergency medical services were called for left lower-leg pain and swelling. Symptoms began approximately two hours before arrival and became noticeable while he was walking around his home. He describes a tight, stretched sensation in the skin with aching discomfort that worsens when bearing weight or walking. He has also noticed mild redness and warmth of the affected lower leg compared with the opposite side. He does not recall a fall, impact, twisting event, insect bite, or other injury. He reports no similar current symptoms in the right leg. He has a history of recurrent peeling and cracking between the toes consistent with athlete’s foot, including recent irritation on the left. A close family member previously experienced a blood clot in a leg. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, fever, or chills.

Symptoms: I have pain, swelling, redness, warmth, and skin tightness in my left lower leg, along with a mild feverish feeling.
Case_History_Text: I’m 28 and work at a daycare. A coworker brought me to the emergency department because my left lower leg has become painful and swollen over roughly the last six hours. The skin looks red, feels warmer than the other leg, and seems tight, especially around my calf and ankle. The discomfort is a steady soreness that is more noticeable when I stand or walk. I do not remember bumping, twisting, or otherwise injuring it, and I have not noticed the same problem in my right leg. I feel mildly feverish but have not had shaking chills. I have diabetes, use estrogen therapy, and recently returned from a several-hour flight.

Symptoms: Unilateral lower-leg pain, swelling, redness, warmth, and skin tightness for three hours; itchy, peeling skin between toes.
Case_History_Text: 61-y/o man, warehouse supervisor, arrived to ED via EMS with spouse. Reports 3 hrs of increasing pain and swelling of the left lower leg, with localized redness, warmth, and a tight sensation of the skin. Denies known injury or fall. Symptoms began while at work and have persisted at rest. States the leg feels heavy and tender with walking. Reports recurrent itchy, peeling skin and small cracks between the toes. No similar symptoms in the opposite leg. Alert, speaking clearly, ambulatory with discomfort.

Symptoms: One-sided lower-leg pain and swelling, skin tightness, redness, and pain with walking.
Case_History_Text: I am her cousin and neighbor, and I brought her to the emergency department after her left lower leg became painful and swollen over the past 45 minutes. She says the skin feels unusually tight, and I noticed mild redness around the calf and ankle. Walking makes the pain worse, so she has been taking short, careful steps. She does not remember falling, twisting the leg, bumping it, or having any other injury. She is 66 and currently attends college full-time. She returned several days ago from a long flight. She has also recently complained of itching and cracked skin between the toes from athlete’s foot. She has not noticed similar symptoms in the other leg.

Symptoms: One-sided calf pain, swelling, redness, warmth, skin tightness, and a mild feverish feeling for one day.
Case_History_Text: I am a 54-year-old janitor. Over the past day, my left calf has become increasingly sore and swollen. The skin feels tight, warm, and looks red compared with my other leg. I have felt mildly feverish but have not checked my temperature. I do not remember a fall, twist, impact, or other injury. I did notice a small scrape on that calf several days ago while working. I am obese and recently had surgery. The discomfort is present at rest and is more noticeable when I stand or walk. My coworker became concerned because the swelling seemed worse during our shift, called EMS, and came with me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: Right lower-leg pain, unilateral swelling, redness, and warmth since last night; no remembered injury.
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We have a 30-year-old woman who works at a daycare, brought to the emergency department with a coworker. She reports right calf and lower-leg pain with swelling that began last night and has persisted today. The affected area appears mildly red and feels warmer than the opposite leg. She does not remember twisting, falling, being struck, or sustaining any other injury. Walking increases the discomfort, though she remains able to bear weight. She reports that a close family member previously had a blood clot.
Model_Diagnosis: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the right lower extremity

Symptoms: unilateral left leg pain; left calf swelling; localized erythema; warmth; pain with walking
Case_History_Text: A 44-year-old woman who works as a nurse presented to the emergency department with a coworker for left lower-leg pain and swelling that began last night. She first noticed a tight, aching sensation near the end of her shift, followed by increased calf fullness and redness by morning. The discomfort is constant, worsens with walking and ankle movement, and has made it difficult to complete routine tasks. She reports warmth over the affected area but denies drainage, an open wound, known insect bite, or recent direct injury. She has had no similar episode previously. She denies fever, shaking chills, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, dizziness, or fainting. She has not recently undergone surgery or prolonged bed rest, though her work involves long periods on her feet. Her father was previously hospitalized for unexplained leg swelling after extended travel. She takes no daily medications and reports no recent medication changes.

Symptoms: unilateral left lower-leg pain; swelling; erythema; warmth; skin tightness; pain with walking
Case_History_Text: I’m 40 and work as a high school coach. Since yesterday evening, my left calf and lower leg have been hurting and swelling on and off. This morning the skin looked red, felt warmer than the other side, and seemed tight enough that my pant leg was uncomfortable. Walking makes the pain worse, so during practice I had to sit down. My adult child became concerned when the swelling increased and called EMS, and they came with me to the emergency department. I have diabetes and had abdominal surgery about three weeks ago. I’ve been less active than usual while recovering, though I started returning to work this week. I don’t recall twisting the leg, being struck, or noticing a cut or insect bite.

Symptoms: unilateral left calf pain; left leg swelling; erythema; skin tightness; warmth; mild feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: 44F software engineer presents to ED with coworker for L calf pain and swelling developing over most of today. Reports skin feels tight; coworker noticed redness. Area is warm and tender. Pt felt mildly feverish at work but denies measured temp. No fall, twisting, or other injury recalled. Has small superficial scrape on posterior calf from gardening several days ago. Hx diabetes. Had outpatient abdominal surgery 2 wks ago and has been less active while recovering. Denies similar prior episode. Ambulatory with discomfort. T 99.6 F, HR 94, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA.

Symptoms: left calf pain; unilateral leg swelling; redness; warmth; mild feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: My brother is 36 and currently unemployed. He called me this evening because his left calf had suddenly become sore and swollen over about two hours. He said the skin looked red and felt warmer than the other leg, and he felt mildly feverish, though he had not checked his temperature. The pain was worse when standing and walking, and his shoe and trouser leg felt tighter on that side. He returned three days ago from a flight lasting several hours and had mostly stayed home since then. He does not recall hitting the leg, twisting it, or being bitten. Because I live across town and could not reach him quickly, EMS was called. He arrived alone at the emergency department, alert and able to describe the symptoms.

Symptoms: left lower-leg pain; unilateral swelling; redness; warmth; tight-feeling skin; mild feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 68-year-old accountant and came alone to the emergency department because my left lower leg became painful and swollen about six hours ago. The skin from my ankle toward my calf looks redder than the other side, feels warm, and seems unusually tight. I have felt mildly feverish but have not checked my temperature. I do not recall falling, twisting the leg, or being bitten. For the past week, I have had itchy, peeling skin and small cracks between the toes on that foot. My sister was previously hospitalized after developing sudden swelling in one leg. I spent most of today seated finishing quarterly reports, although that is fairly typical for me.

Symptoms: unilateral left leg pain; left calf swelling; skin tightness; redness; warmth; mild feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 36-year-old man who works as an accountant; his neighbor called EMS and accompanied him after noticing he was limping. Over the last three hours, he developed increasing pain and swelling of the left lower leg, with tight-feeling skin, patchy redness, and warmth. He reports feeling mildly feverish but does not recall any injury, bite, or unusual exertion. He has been sitting longer than usual during tax-season work. He reports that an uncle previously had a leg clot. He denies recent surgery and is not taking estrogen therapy. He was alert and ambulatory with assistance during transport.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute deep vein thrombosis of the left lower extremity

Symptoms: unilateral left leg pain; left lower-leg swelling; erythema; pain with walking; mild feverish feeling
Case_History_Text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with her spouse for left lower-leg pain and swelling noticed over the past 45 minutes. She first became aware of tightness around the calf while getting up from the couch, followed by increasing soreness and visible puffiness. Walking and bearing weight make the discomfort more pronounced, although she remains able to ambulate. Her spouse noticed mild redness over the lower calf and ankle compared with the opposite side. She reports feeling slightly feverish but has not measured her temperature and denies shaking chills. She does not recall a fall, direct injury, strenuous exercise, or an insect bite. She has not noticed drainage, bleeding, or an open wound. The discomfort is described as a steady ache rather than burning or electric pain. She denies similar prior episodes. She is currently unemployed and reports spending much of the day at home. Her background is notable for obesity.

Symptoms: painful area of skin redness and warmth on the left lower leg; fever; chills; rapidly worsening pain
Case_History_Text: A 23-year-old woman who works as a welder presents to the emergency department with her 19-year-old stepdaughter for evaluation of a painful red area on the left lower leg. She first noticed mild tenderness and a small patch of redness near the shin after work yesterday, without a known burn, puncture, or other injury.
