This evening she developed subjective fever and intermittent chills. During the past 45 minutes, the pain has intensified and the redness appears to have spread slightly, prompting her visit. She describes the pain as deep, constant, and more severe than she would expect from the current skin appearance, although she remains able to bear weight. She denies numbness, weakness, drainage, blistering, or similar prior episodes. She has obesity but reports no diabetes, immune disorder, recent hospitalization, surgery, or injection drug use. She took acetaminophen before arrival with little relief.

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; chills; fatigue; rapidly increasing swelling; puncture wound; chronic foot wounds
Case_History_Text: I’m 47 and a full-time college student. Since yesterday morning, the skin around my left lower leg has become red, warm, swollen, and increasingly painful. The swelling spread from near my ankle toward my calf over the day, and walking is uncomfortable. Last night I felt feverish, had shaking chills, and was unusually tired. About a week ago, I stepped on a small piece of metal while cleaning out our garage and didn’t get the puncture checked because it seemed minor. I also have a couple of chronic sores near that ankle that sometimes reopen. My spouse became worried when the redness expanded and I looked worse this evening, so they called EMS and came with me to the emergency department. I haven’t noticed any drainage or numbness.

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; chills; fatigue; swelling
Case_History_Text: 49F software engineer presents to ED with adult daughter for increasing pain, redness, warmth, and mild swelling of L lower leg since last night. Reports feverishness, chills, and fatigue. Pain is more intense than the limited visible redness would suggest, though she remains ambulatory. Pt recalls stepping on a small metal garden stake 3 days ago; puncture was rinsed briefly but otherwise neglected. Hx diabetes and a prior similar skin infection several years ago. Denies recent surgery, animal bite, or known sick contacts. Alert, uncomfortable but conversant at triage.

Symptoms: painful red swollen skin around a puncture wound; fever; chills; warmth; tenderness
Case_History_Text: My father is a 50-year-old security guard who came to the emergency department with me after I called EMS. Yesterday evening, he began having spells of chills and fever along with aching pain in his right lower leg. The symptoms have come and gone overnight, but the area has become increasingly red, warm, swollen, and tender today. He can still move the ankle, although walking makes the pain worse. A few days ago, he stepped on a sharp piece of metal while checking a poorly lit loading area at work. He rinsed the small puncture on his heel but did not have it examined and continued working. This afternoon he seemed more tired than usual and the redness appeared to be spreading upward, so I called for help.
Model_Diagnosis: Cellulitis of the right lower extremity

Symptoms: red, warm skin on left lower leg; increasing leg pain; fever; fatigue; mild swelling
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 48-year-old warehouse supervisor and came to the emergency department alone after my left lower leg became red, warm, and painful over most of today. I noticed a small irritated spot near my ankle before work, but the redness and swelling have gradually spread upward. I feel feverish and unusually tired. The pain is steady and somewhat stronger than I would expect from how the skin looks, although I can still walk with a limp. I do not recall a major injury, but my work boots sometimes rub that area. I have obesity and had a similar skin infection several years ago that improved after medical care. I have not noticed drainage, numbness, or discoloration.

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; fatigue; rapidly increasing swelling
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 31-year-old man from his apartment after he called for worsening left lower-leg pain and swelling over roughly two hours. He is a librarian and arrived alone. The lower shin is red, warm, tender, and increasingly swollen; he says the pain feels more intense than the visible skin changes suggest, though he can still move the ankle and toes. He reports fatigue and fever today. Last week he stepped on a small metal staple and did not seek care for the puncture wound. History includes diabetes. Door vitals: temperature 38.2°C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 128/76, respirations 18, oxygen saturation 99%.

Symptoms: painful red swollen skin; fever; chills; fatigue
Case_History_Text: A 63-year-old woman who works as an accountant presented to the emergency department with her adult daughter for approximately six hours of worsening pain, redness, and swelling along the outer aspect of her right lower leg. She first noticed soreness while leaving work, followed by spreading warmth and erythema during the evening. She describes the pain as a steady 6/10 ache that increases with walking and direct pressure. She reports subjective fever, intermittent chills, and unusual fatigue but denies vomiting, shortness of breath, or recent prolonged travel. Three days earlier, she punctured the same area on a sharp piece of garden wire while clearing debris at home. She rinsed it briefly but did not otherwise clean or cover it because the wound seemed minor. Since then, there had been little discomfort until today. She has not noticed purulent drainage, blistering, numbness, or loss of function. Her daughter became concerned when the redness expanded beyond the original puncture site.
Model_Diagnosis: Nonpurulent cellulitis of the right lower leg

Symptoms: painful red skin on the left lower leg; fever; chills; warmth; swelling
Case_History_Text: I’m 52 and manage a retail store. About three hours ago, while closing up, I noticed a sore, warm patch on my left lower leg near a small crack in the skin by my ankle. The redness and swelling have spread a little since then. I started feeling feverish and had chills, and the pain became stronger than I expected from how the area looks, though I can still walk with a limp. My adult daughter thought I looked unwell and called EMS, so she came with me to the emergency department. I have diabetes and I’m overweight. I don’t remember an injury, bite, or burn, and I haven’t noticed drainage or numbness.
Model_Diagnosis: Cellulitis of the left lower leg

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; chills; fatigue; rapidly increasing swelling
Case_History_Text: Triage: 56F office administrator presents alone for worsening redness, warmth, and swelling of R lower leg, with noticeable spread over past 45 min. Reports aching/burning pain, feverishness, chills, and fatigue today. States she stepped on a small metal staple through her shoe last week and did not seek care; puncture near ankle remains crusted. Also has a chronic shallow sore on the same shin. Had a similar skin infection several years ago that improved with outpatient care. Ambulatory but limping. Denies recent surgery or known injury beyond puncture. T 38.2 C, HR 98, BP 134/82, RR 18.

Symptoms: painful red skin on the lower leg; swelling; warmth; fever; chills; fatigue; chronic open sores
Case_History_Text: I’m his 19-year-old stepdaughter, and I came with him after we called EMS this evening. He is 22 and manages a busy retail store, where he spends most of each shift on his feet. Over the past day, an area around one of the chronic sores on his right lower leg has become red, warm, swollen, and increasingly painful. The redness seemed a little larger by late afternoon, and he began limping. He felt feverish at home, had several bouts of chills, and was unusually tired, so I convinced him not to finish closing the store. He has had similar slow-healing wounds before but says this episode became sore more quickly. He denies a recent major injury and has been awake, coherent, and able to answer questions since EMS arrived.
Model_Diagnosis: Cellulitis of the right lower leg

Symptoms: red, warm, swollen skin on the left lower leg; increasing pain; fever; chills; rapid swelling
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 23-year-old woman and restaurant cook, writing from the emergency department. My neighbor brought me because the skin around a small scrape on my left shin has become red, hot, tender, and noticeably swollen since last night. The redness seems to have spread over several hours, and the pain has increased, especially when I stand or walk during a shift. I developed fever and chills overnight and feel tired and mildly nauseated, but I have not vomited. I had a similar skin infection on the other leg about two years ago that improved after an urgent-care visit. I also have diabetes and sometimes miss doses of my daily medication when work gets hectic.
Model_Diagnosis: Cellulitis of the left lower leg

Symptoms: painful red skin lesion; rapidly increasing swelling; fever; chills; pain greater than expected from visible skin changes
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 30-year-old man from home after his coworker called 911. He works as a home health aide and reports intermittent pain and redness around a chronic wound on his left lower leg since yesterday evening. This morning the swelling increased over several hours, with subjective fever and shaking chills. He says the pain is more intense than the skin changes appear, though he remains able to move the ankle and bear limited weight. History includes diabetes, obesity, and recurrent slow-healing foot and leg wounds. He was alert throughout transport, with stable, non-diagnostic door vital signs.

Symptoms: painful red skin; swelling; warmth; fever; chills; tenderness
Case_History_Text: A 34-year-old woman who works at a daycare presented to the emergency department with a neighbor for worsening pain, redness, and warmth over her left lower leg. She first noticed a small tender area near the ankle early this morning after getting dressed for work. Over most of the day, the discomfort intensified and the redness spread upward several centimeters despite rest and elevation. She describes a constant deep ache with sharper pain when walking or when the area is touched; at times, the discomfort has seemed more intense than she expected from the visible skin changes. She reports feeling feverish with intermittent chills this afternoon but denies vomiting, fainting, chest discomfort, or shortness of breath. She does not recall a specific injury, although she noticed a tiny superficial crack in the skin near the heel several days ago. Her history is notable for obesity. She has not taken antibiotics recently and reports no prior similar episode.

Symptoms: painful red skin on lower leg; fever; fatigue; swelling; warmth
Case_History_Text: I’m 58 and coach at the local high school. About two hours ago, after getting home from practice, I noticed a warm, red, swollen patch along my left shin near a small scrape. The pain has become steady and feels somewhat stronger than I would expect from how the skin looks, though I can still move my ankle and walk with a limp. I’ve also felt feverish and unusually tired since this afternoon. My neighbor became concerned when I started shivering and called EMS, then came with me to the emergency department. I had a similar skin infection on the other leg several years ago that improved after medical care. I’m obese, but otherwise I haven’t noticed drainage, numbness, or a recent major injury.

Symptoms: painful red skin; rapid swelling; fever; chills; fatigue
Case_History_Text: 30F bus driver presents to ED with adult daughter for ~6 hrs of increasing redness, warmth, swelling, and pain of L lower leg. Reports chills, fever, and marked fatigue since finishing afternoon route. Pain 7/10, worse with standing but tolerates light touch. Notes stepping on a metal staple through her shoe 3 days ago; cleaned it briefly and did not seek care. Had a similar localized skin infection 2 yrs ago that resolved. Hx obesity, otherwise denies major illness. T 38.1 C, HR 102, BP 128/76, RR 18. Alert, ambulatory, appears uncomfortable.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the left lower leg

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; fatigue; rapidly increasing swelling
Case_History_Text: My brother is a 56-year-old farmer with diabetes. His neighbor came with him to the emergency department after calling EMS from the farm. About three hours ago, he noticed a sore, red patch around a small scrape on his left shin. Since then, the area has become warmer and more swollen, spreading toward his calf faster than he expected. He says the pain is steady and fairly strong, especially when he stands, but he can still move his ankle and toes. He felt feverish and unusually tired while finishing chores and had to sit down. He does not recall an animal bite or chemical exposure. The scrape may have happened while repairing a fence yesterday, but it had not bothered him until this afternoon.

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; rapid swelling; warmth; fatigue; pain greater than expected from visible skin changes
Case_History_Text: Message for the emergency team: I am a 57-year-old librarian and came to the emergency department with my neighbor. A few days ago, I stepped on a sharp piece of garden wire and neglected the small puncture near my right ankle. The area became red, warm, and painful yesterday, and I have felt feverish and unusually tired today. During the past 45 minutes, the swelling has spread quickly up my lower leg and the pain has intensified. It seems somewhat worse than the skin looks, although I can still move my ankle and toes. I have obesity but no recent surgery or hospital stay. I rinsed the wound when it happened but did not seek care or take medication for it.

Symptoms: painful red skin; fever; chills; fatigue; rapid lower-leg swelling
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 65-year-old man from home after his adult daughter called for worsening redness, warmth, and swelling of his right lower leg over the past day. He reports steady, moderately severe pain that has increased as the swelling spread, along with fever, chills, and fatigue. He works at a daycare and was unable to finish his shift today. He has obesity and chronic wounds around both ankles; his daughter says he had a similar episode several years ago. No known recent injury, though he noticed drainage from a small ankle sore yesterday. He remained alert during transport.

Symptoms: painful skin redness; fever; rapid swelling; warmth; fatigue
Case_History_Text: A 59-year-old woman who works as a construction foreman presents to the emergency department with a coworker for a painful, red area on her left lower leg that began last night. She first noticed tenderness near a small scrape over the shin after removing her work boot. By early morning, the redness and swelling had spread toward the calf, and the skin felt increasingly warm and tight. She reports a fever at home with chills and unusual fatigue, prompting her coworker to drive her in rather than let her finish the shift. The pain is constant, moderate to severe, and worsens with walking or pressure, though she remains able to bear weight. She has not noticed drainage, blistering, numbness, or loss of movement. Several years ago, she had a similar skin infection on the opposite leg that improved after medical care. She denies a recent operation, animal bite, prolonged travel, or known chemical exposure at the job site.
Model_Diagnosis: Cellulitis of the left lower extremity

Symptoms: red, warm, swollen skin on the lower leg; worsening pain; fever; chills
Case_History_Text: I’m 50 and work as a cook at a neighborhood restaurant. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had pain on and off in my right lower leg near the ankle. I first noticed a small red, warm patch after my shift, and today it looks a little more swollen. The pain has become sharper and sometimes seems worse than I would expect from how the skin looks, though I can still walk with a limp. I felt feverish overnight and had chills this afternoon. I don’t remember cutting myself, but I’m on my feet in a hot kitchen all day and sometimes get small cracks in my skin. I have diabetes and my sugars are not always well controlled. My adult child became concerned when I started shivering and called EMS, then came with me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: left lower-leg redness and warmth; increasing swelling; pain; fever; chills; puncture wound
Case_History_Text: 35F farmer arrives to ED with coworker for worsening L lower-leg pain, redness, and swelling developing over most of today. Reports fever/chills and swelling that increased quickly this afternoon. Pain is significant and somewhat greater than the visible skin changes suggest, though she remains able to bear weight. Stepped on a sharp piece of fencing last week and did not seek care; small neglected puncture near ankle with scant drainage. Hx diabetes and recurrent slow-healing foot wounds. Denies recent surgery or known insect bite. Alert, uncomfortable but conversational at triage. T 38.2 C, HR 102, BP 128/76, RR 18.

Symptoms: painful red swollen skin on the left lower leg; fever; chills; fatigue
Case_History_Text: I came with my father, a 57-year-old daycare worker, after I called EMS this evening. About two hours earlier, he noticed a sore, warm red patch near his left ankle that seemed to spread upward across the lower leg. He describes the pain as strong and constant, especially when standing, but he can still move the ankle and toes. He became feverish, had shaking chills, and seemed much more tired than usual. There is a small cracked area of skin near his heel, though he does not remember a specific injury or bite. He has diabetes and says his glucose control has been inconsistent lately. He was well enough to work earlier today and has not had similar symptoms before.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the left lower leg

Symptoms: fever; chills; rapidly increasing redness and swelling of the left lower leg; worsening pain; warmth around a puncture wound
Case_History_Text: Hello emergency team, I am a 57-year-old woman who drives for a rideshare service. My neighbor brought me to the emergency department because, over roughly six hours, my left lower leg has become red, hot, swollen, and increasingly painful. I have also felt feverish and had several bouts of chills. The pain sometimes feels stronger than I would expect from how the skin looks, although I can still move my ankle and walk with difficulty. Last week I stepped on a small piece of metal while clearing trash from my car and neglected the puncture after rinsing it briefly. The area had seemed fine until today. I have obesity but no recent surgery or similar skin problem.

Symptoms: painful skin redness of the left lower leg; rapid swelling; fever; chills
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 45-year-old man, a city bus driver, after his neighbor called 911. Over the last three hours he developed increasing redness, warmth, swelling, and pain around a chronic sore on his left shin, along with fever and shaking chills. He rates the pain 8/10 and says it feels somewhat worse than the limited skin changes suggest, though he remains able to move the ankle and toes. He has diabetes and reports a similar leg infection several years ago. No known recent trauma or bite. On arrival he was alert; BP 138/84, pulse 104, respirations 20, temperature 38.2°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.

Symptoms: painful red skin on left lower leg; fever; chills; swelling; warmth
Case_History_Text: A 23-year-old woman who works as a retail manager presents alone to the emergency department for rapidly increasing pain, redness, and warmth of the left lower leg noticed over the past 45 minutes. She first became aware of soreness while closing her store, then saw an expanding red area around a small heel blister caused by new work shoes. The pain is constant, rated 7/10, and worsens with walking or direct pressure. She reports feeling feverish with intermittent chills but denies vomiting, dizziness, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, or recent injury beyond the blister. She has not noticed pus, bleeding, or a foul odor. Her history is notable for diabetes, and she acknowledges that her glucose control has been inconsistent during several weeks of late shifts. She denies prior similar episodes, recent hospitalization, water exposure, injection drug use, or known sick contacts. She took acetaminophen shortly before arrival without meaningful relief.

Symptoms: low back pain; subjective fever; difficulty urinating; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: A 57-year-old woman who works as a librarian presents to the emergency department with a neighbor for worsening low back pain. She reports several days of a dull ache across the lower lumbar region after repeatedly lifting boxes of returned books, with a marked increase in intensity over the past 45 minutes while sitting at home. The pain is constant, worse with movement, and occasionally extends into both buttocks without a clear shooting component. This evening she felt chilled and warm but did not measure her temperature. She also describes difficulty initiating urination since this afternoon, although she has passed a small amount and denies burning or visible blood. She notes brief tingling in both feet but no definite weakness, fall, saddle numbness, or loss of bowel control. Two weeks ago, she had a skin abscess on her upper thigh treated as an outpatient; drainage has reportedly stopped. She denies recent spinal procedures or major trauma.

Symptoms: lower back pain; muscle spasms; intermittent leg numbness; subjective fever
Case_History_Text: I’m a 42-year-old farmer, and since yesterday I’ve had worsening pain across my lower back. It started after a long morning moving feed sacks and fixing a gate, but I don’t remember one specific injury. The pain feels deep and tight, with sudden spasms when I stand or twist. Overnight I felt hot and sweaty, although I didn’t check my temperature. This morning, both legs felt briefly numb and heavy while I was walking to the barn, so I sat down. I can still move them, but the tingling comes and goes. I haven’t lost control of my bladder or bowels. My diabetes has been poorly controlled lately because I sometimes miss medication during busy weeks. My coworker became concerned when I struggled to climb into the truck and called EMS; he came with me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: low back pain since last night; subjective fever; intermittent leg numbness; urinary hesitancy; fatigue; pain worse at night
Case_History_Text: 66-y/o woman farmer presents to ED with spouse for midline low back pain starting last night after moving feed sacks and repairing a gate. Pain persisted overnight, worse with turning and walking, and intermittently radiates into both buttocks. Reports fatigue, feeling feverish, brief numbness in the left leg, and difficulty initiating urine this AM; denies incontinence, saddle numbness, or recent fall. Hx poorly controlled diabetes. Recently completed outpatient medication for a drained skin abscess on upper thigh; area reportedly improving. Ambulatory with slow, guarded gait. T 37.7 C, HR 94, BP 148/82, RR 18.

Symptoms: intermittent low back pain; night pain; feeling feverish; occasional leg tingling; difficulty starting urination
Case_History_Text: I’m his older brother and used to work with him at a moving company. Although he is currently unemployed, he agreed to help another former coworker move furniture yesterday. Since yesterday evening, he has had low back pain that comes and goes but became bad enough overnight to keep him awake. He says it is worse when bending or standing up, and once or twice he noticed tingling down the back of his right leg. This morning he felt hot and sweaty, though we did not check his temperature. He also said it took longer than usual to start urinating, without loss of bladder control. Last week he had a sore, draining patch of skin near his left knee that seems to be healing. His coworker called EMS when the pain intensified and came with us to the emergency department.

Symptoms: mid-to-lower back pain; subjective fever; muscle spasms; difficulty urinating; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: Hello emergency team, I’m a 56-year-old woman and a returning college student. My neighbor brought me to the emergency department because I’ve had worsening mid-to-lower back pain for most of today. It started as tightness after carrying a backpack and sitting through a long class, but it now comes in strong spasms even when I’m resting. I felt feverish and chilled this evening, although I did not check my temperature. Twice today I had trouble starting urination, and I’ve noticed brief tingling down the back of my left thigh without clear weakness. I have diabetes and was previously told I have osteoporosis. I have not fallen or had any recent procedure. The pain is making it difficult to walk normally or find a comfortable position.

Symptoms: severe midline low-back pain; muscle spasms; urinary hesitancy; fatigue; subjective leg tingling; night pain; possible fever
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 57-year-old man from home with his spouse after she called for sudden worsening of low-back pain over about two hours. He is a construction foreman but denies a specific injury today. Pain woke him overnight and now comes with tight spasms, fatigue, intermittent tingling in both legs, and difficulty starting urination. He felt warm at home but did not check his temperature. He recently completed outpatient treatment for a drained skin abscess and reports another minor skin infection last month. History includes osteoporosis. He remained alert and able to move all extremities during transport.

Symptoms: acute low back pain; fatigue; chills; difficulty urinating; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: A 75-year-old woman, a retired accountant, presents to the emergency department accompanied by a former coworker for roughly six hours of worsening low back pain. She first noticed a deep ache after carrying several grocery bags and later developed sharper pain with standing, twisting, or walking. The discomfort is centered in the lower lumbar region without a fall or direct injury. She reports unusual fatigue, mild chills, and feeling warm at home but did not measure her temperature. She has also had difficulty initiating urination this evening, passing only small amounts despite feeling the urge. She describes intermittent tingling in both thighs but denies persistent numbness, leg weakness, saddle-area sensory loss, or loss of bowel control. She has a history of recurring disc-related back problems, although she says this episode feels more intense and less responsive to rest. She reports no recent spinal procedure or known skin infection. At triage she is alert, uncomfortable with movement, and hemodynamically stable.

Symptoms: lower back pain; muscle spasms; feeling feverish; fatigue; intermittent tingling in the right leg; night pain
Case_History_Text: I’m 41 and work at a daycare. For the last three hours, I’ve had worsening pain across my lower back, with tight spasms that sometimes shoot toward my right buttock. It started after I twisted while lifting a child from the floor, but it has not eased with rest and feels worse when I lie still. I’ve also felt unusually tired and a little feverish, although I did not check my temperature. My right foot has tingled on and off, but I can walk and have not had trouble controlling my bladder or bowels. I have diabetes and recently finished caring for a sore, reddened patch of skin on my calf. The pain woke me after I tried to nap, so my neighbor called EMS and came with me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: acute low back pain; subjective fever; fatigue; bilateral leg numbness; pain worse at night
Case_History_Text: 40-y/o woman, auto mechanic, brought to ED by coworker for severe midline low-back pain starting 45 min PTA while lifting a toolbox. Pain radiates across lower back and is worse with movement; reports brief numbness in both thighs but walked in without assistance. Felt feverish and unusually tired since yesterday, with pain disturbing sleep overnight. Hx prior lumbar disc problems; also spends several hrs/day doing shop paperwork with poor ergonomics. Osteoporosis noted in prior history. Denies recent fall, bowel/bladder changes, or saddle numbness. T 37.8 C, HR 96, BP 132/78.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute osteoporotic lumbar vertebral compression fracture

Symptoms: lower back pain; muscle spasms; feeling feverish; difficulty starting urination; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: My 34-year-old brother, who works as a nurse, came to the emergency department alone by ambulance after calling EMS from his apartment. Since yesterday morning, he has had worsening pain across his lower back with tight, cramping spasms. He first thought he had strained it while repositioning a patient during a busy shift. By evening he felt feverish and sweaty, although he did not check his temperature. Today he mentioned brief tingling in both legs and said it was taking longer than usual to start urinating, but he has still been able to walk and pass urine. He has not reported a fall or other injury. About two weeks ago, he had a painful skin abscess near his waist treated at an outpatient clinic; he says the area now looks much better.

Symptoms: mid-back pain since last night; fatigue; feeling feverish; pain at night; difficulty starting urination; intermittent tingling in the right leg
Case_History_Text: Hello emergency team, I’m a 38-year-old daycare worker and came in with a coworker because my back pain has steadily worsened since last night. It began after a busy shift that included lifting several toddlers and moving a small play table, but I do not remember a specific injury. The pain is centered in my mid-to-lower back, kept me awake, and is worse when I bend or walk. I feel unusually tired and feverish, though I did not check my temperature. This morning I had trouble starting my urine stream and noticed brief tingling down my right leg, without loss of bladder control. I have diabetes and recently finished care for an infected sore on my lower abdomen. I have not had similar pain before.

Symptoms: intermittent low back pain; muscle spasm; fatigue; subjective fever; episodic leg numbness
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 47-year-old man from his office after a coworker called for worsening low back pain. Symptoms have come and gone since yesterday evening, with tight spasms and brief numbness extending into both thighs when standing. He reports fatigue and feeling feverish overnight but did not check his temperature. He denies a fall, heavy lifting, bowel or bladder changes, or persistent weakness. History includes diabetes, prior disc problems, and a recent skin abscess treated as an outpatient. He was able to walk to the stretcher with assistance. Coworker is at bedside. Transport was uneventful.

Symptoms: midline lower back pain; muscle spasms; fatigue; subjective fever; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: A 53-year-old woman employed as a postal worker presents to the emergency department with a coworker for lower back pain that began this morning and has progressively worsened through the day. She spends much of her shift sorting mail and entering routing information at a poorly adjusted workstation, and she initially attributed the discomfort to prolonged sitting and repeated twisting. The pain is described as a deep, constant ache near the midline with intermittent tightening or spasms, worse when rising from a chair or bending. She also reports unusual fatigue, feeling intermittently warm, and brief tingling down the back of her right thigh, although she remains able to walk. She denies a fall or direct injury. She has not measured her temperature. She reports no urinary retention, incontinence, saddle numbness, or persistent leg weakness. Her coworker encouraged evaluation after noticing that she appeared uncomfortable and had difficulty completing her usual duties.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute lumbar strain with muscle spasm

Symptoms: mid-back pain; muscle spasms; feeling feverish; fatigue; intermittent tingling in the right leg
Case_History_Text: I’m a 30-year-old office administrator, and about two hours ago I developed a deep ache in the middle of my back while moving a box of printer paper at work. It has become sharper and keeps tightening into spasms, especially when I twist or try to stand straight. I also feel unusually tired and feverish, and I noticed brief tingling down my right leg, though I can still walk and haven’t lost bladder or bowel control. A coworker called EMS because the pain was getting worse, and I came to the emergency department alone. Last week, I had a painful skin abscess near my left hip drained at a clinic and was given medication. The area is smaller now but still slightly sore.

Symptoms: acute low back pain; muscle spasm; subjective fever; fatigue; intermittent right-leg tingling; night pain
Case_History_Text: 40F farmer presents alone to ED with ~6 hrs of worsening midline/ R low-back pain and tight spasms, first noticed after moving feed bags and now present at rest. Pain woke her overnight. Reports fatigue, chills, and temp 100.4°F at home. Intermittent tingling down posterior R thigh; denies leg weakness, saddle numbness, falls, or bowel/bladder change. Hx diabetes. Had a draining skin abscess on L calf treated outpatient 2 wks ago; says area is improving. Ambulatory but guarded. T 37.7°C, HR 96, BP 138/84, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA.

Symptoms: low back pain; pain worse at night and with movement; feeling feverish; difficulty starting urination; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: My 30-year-old brother was brought to the emergency department alone by EMS after calling from his apartment. He works as a mechanic and had spent the afternoon bending over an engine and helping lift a heavy transmission. About three hours ago, he developed deep lower back pain that has steadily worsened and is keeping him from resting. He told me by phone that he felt hot and chilled, though he had not checked his temperature. He also mentioned brief tingling down one leg and trouble getting his urine stream started, without loss of bladder control or definite weakness. Last week he had a tender, draining spot on his upper thigh that he thought was an infected ingrown hair. He has had occasional work-related back soreness before, but says this episode feels more intense.

Symptoms: mid-back pain; muscle spasm; fatigue; night pain; subjective fever; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: Hello emergency team, I am a 71-year-old home health aide and came in with a coworker because my mid-to-lower back pain suddenly became much stronger about 45 minutes ago while I was finishing paperwork. The pain feels deep and tight, with spasms, and has bothered me at night for the last two evenings. I have also felt unusually tired and slightly feverish, although I did not check my temperature. During the ride here, I noticed brief tingling in both legs, but I can still walk and have had no loss of bladder or bowel control. I spend long periods doing office documentation at a poorly adjusted desk. Last week, I completed care for a red, draining sore on my left forearm, which now looks improved.

Symptoms: low back pain; fatigue; subjective fever; intermittent leg numbness; difficulty urinating; pain worse at night
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 73-year-old man from home after his neighbor called due to worsening low back pain since yesterday. He is a retired accountant with years of desk work and poor posture. He reports unusual fatigue, feeling feverish overnight, intermittent numbness in both legs, and difficulty starting his urine stream today. The pain persisted through the night and worsens with movement, though he denies a fall or other trauma. History includes poorly controlled diabetes and a recent draining skin sore on his lower leg that has mostly closed. He was alert and able to walk slowly with assistance.

Symptoms: mid-to-lower back pain; subjective fever; night pain; intermittent tingling in both feet
Case_History_Text: A 54-year-old woman who works as a retail manager presents to the emergency department with a neighbor for back pain that began last night. She spent much of the prior day completing inventory reports at a poorly arranged office workstation but does not recall a specific strain, fall, or other injury. The pain is centered over the mid-to-lower back, remains present at rest, and kept her awake overnight. It becomes sharper with twisting, standing from a chair, and walking. She felt feverish and chilled during the night but did not measure her temperature. This morning she noticed brief tingling in both feet while getting out of bed; the sensation has recurred intermittently without clear weakness or difficulty bearing weight. She denies saddle numbness, loss of bladder or bowel control, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, cough, or recent procedures. She reports occasional mild back stiffness after long office shifts, though never pain of this intensity or duration.

Symptoms: intermittent lower back pain; feeling feverish; fatigue; back muscle spasms; occasional leg tingling
Case_History_Text: I’m 61 and work as a restaurant cook. Since yesterday evening, I’ve had pain across my lower back that comes and goes, with tight spasms that sometimes stop me in my tracks. It started after a busy shift when I was lifting stock pots and boxes, but I don’t remember one specific injury. Overnight I felt feverish and unusually tired, though I didn’t check my temperature. This morning, I noticed occasional tingling down the back of my left thigh, similar to what I’ve had with old disc trouble, but I can still walk. I haven’t lost control of my bladder or bowels. My diabetes has been poorly controlled lately. I live alone, so my neighbor became worried, called EMS, and came with me to the emergency department.

Symptoms: mid-to-low back pain; muscle spasm; subjective fever; intermittent leg numbness; night pain
Case_History_Text: 36F welder presents to ED with adult daughter for worsening mid-to-low back pain since this morning, now preventing sleep. Reports tight spasms after lifting metal stock at work; also recently assigned several weeks of office scheduling with poor chair setup. Felt feverish/chilled this evening but did not check temp. Notes intermittent numbness down the back of the L leg, without weakness, saddle numbness, or bowel/bladder changes. Hx poorly controlled diabetes; osteoporosis mentioned in prior clinic records. Denies fall, recent procedure, or open wound. Ambulatory with guarded gait. T 37.8 C, other door VS stable.

Symptoms: sudden worsening low back pain; feeling feverish; difficulty urinating; intermittent tingling in both legs
Case_History_Text: My dad is 33 and works as a cook at a busy restaurant. About two hours before we arrived, he developed strong pain across his lower back while helping move a box of frozen food near the end of his shift. He tried sitting and stretching, but the pain kept worsening, so I called EMS and came with him to the emergency department. He says he feels feverish and has had brief tingling down both legs, although he was able to walk to the stretcher with help. He has also felt the need to urinate but has passed only a small amount since the pain began. Last week he had a sore, reddened area on his upper thigh that drained on its own. He denies a fall or direct blow to his back.

Symptoms: midline lower back pain; muscle spasms; fatigue; feeling feverish; intermittent leg tingling; pain worse at night
Case_History_Text: Hello, I’m a 41-year-old woman writing from the emergency department, where I arrived alone. About six hours ago, near the end of a rideshare shift, I developed a deep ache in my lower back that has become sharper and more constant. It occasionally tightens into spasms and seems worse when I sit, twist, or try to rest. I have also felt unusually tired and briefly feverish, although I did not check my temperature. Twice, I noticed mild tingling down the back of my left thigh, but I can walk and have not had loss of bladder or bowel control. Before driving, I did office work with poor ergonomics. A clinician once mentioned osteoporosis in my family history, but I have never had a fracture.
Model_Diagnosis: Acute lumbar strain with muscle spasm

Symptoms: lower back pain; subjective fever; intermittent leg numbness; urinary hesitancy; fatigue
Case_History_Text: EMS handoff: We brought in a 65-year-old man who is currently a college student; his neighbor called after three hours of worsening lower back pain that began while he was moving study materials. He reports feeling feverish and unusually tired, with intermittent numbness in both legs and difficulty starting urination tonight. He remained able to walk to the stretcher and denies a fall, direct trauma, or loss of bladder control. History includes diabetes and osteoporosis. He also reports a recently improving skin infection on his forearm. On arrival he is alert, temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96, blood pressure 146/84, and respirations 18.

Symptoms: acute back pain; subjective fever; fatigue; difficulty urinating; intermittent leg tingling
Case_History_Text: A 29-year-old woman who attends college and works part-time at a campus café presents to the emergency department with a coworker for back pain that began approximately 45 minutes before arrival. She first noticed a sharp ache in the midline lower back while twisting to lift a crate of bottled drinks. The pain has persisted at rest and becomes more intense with bending or walking. She reports feeling unusually tired since this morning and intermittently feverish, although she did not check her temperature. Since the pain began, she has had difficulty initiating urination despite feeling that her bladder is full. She also describes brief tingling in both upper thighs but denies persistent numbness, leg weakness, saddle-area sensory change, or loss of bowel or bladder control. She has diabetes and acknowledges that her glucose management has been inconsistent during exams. She denies a fall, recent spinal procedure, known skin infection, or prior similar episode.
